j. The need to appreciate the power of the name of our Lord Jesus. 
966. What do the Holy Bible and the Fathers say about the power of the name of our 
Lord Jesus?  
The Lord Christ granted His name to His disciples, not only so they could perform 
wonders, heal the sick, and cast out dem ons — He assured them of the power of His name 
when He said, “Whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you” (John 16:23). 
Thus, by His name we approach the Father and enjoy His eternal glories. Indeed, the 
seventy apostles came to understand th e power of the name of Jesus, as is evident from 
their words upon their return from their mission: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us 
in Your name!” (Luke 10:17). Isaiah the prophet, in his song of thanksgiving, expressed the 
power of the name of God , saying, “The desire of our soul is for Your name, and for the 
remembrance of You. With my soul I have desired You in the night. Yes, by my spirit 
within me I will seek you early” (Isa. 26:8–9).  
St. John Climacus (of the ladder) says, “Flog your enemies with the name of Jesus, for 
there is no stronger weapon in heaven or earth.”306  
St. Cyril the Great  says, “He among those who do not yet believe in God and who  
despises the name of God confesses the power of the Most Holy One when the rays of the 
truth shine upon him.”

1982) 21.7: p. 172.

continuously. But if it is disturbed, you have to keep reciting the name of the Lord with 
your tongue until the mind gets accustomed to it. Thus, when God sees your labor, He will 
send help to you when He sees the desire of your heart and will thus scatter the thoughts of 
the adversary that fight against the soul.’” 
“It was said that the d emons fought voraciously against Abba Hilarion. One night, he 
began to hear the sound of crying babies, grunting sheep, lowing oxen, wailing of women, 
roaring of lions, shouting of an army and other loud cries. He got scared from all these 
noises even with out seeing anything. Then, he realized that these were evil spirits, so he 
knelt down and made the sign of the cross on his forehead. He was calmed for a moment 
but then, he looked up to see and in the light of the moon, a chariot with soldiers hastening 
above him, so he called on the name of Jesus and the earth opened up suddenly before his 
eyes and swallowed the whole scene. Hilarion then said: ‘The horse and its rider, He has 
thrown into the sea’ (Ex. 15:1), and ‘Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we will 
remember the name of the Lord our God’ (Ps. 20:7).” 
“It was said that Aristaenete, the wife of Elpidius, the Roman governor, on her return 
from a visit to St. Anthony the Great in Egypt, was delayed in Gaza because her three 
children felt il l with a disease known as ‘semi -tertian ague’ [which is like tertian malaria 
that typically flares up or recurs every 48 hours ]. Physicians gave up on a cure and their 
mother kept weeping. She then heard of the presence of a monk in the nearby wilderness, 
so she forgot all about her important status, and driven by her motherhood, she hastened to 
him, riding on a donkey with her maiden servants. She said to the saint: ‘I entreat you for 
the sake of Christ our God, I beg you for the sake of His Cross and Bloo d, to save my three 
children so that His name may be glorified among the pagans.’ At first, the saint refused 
since he had never left his cell before, and he was not accustomed to entering into a house 
or even a city. But the woman cast herself on the grou nd and screamed repeatedly: ‘O 
servant of God, Hilarion, give me back my children. St. Anthony kept them safe in Egypt, 
so you rescue them here in Syria.’ All those who were present wept and so did the saint 
after he declined her request. She did not leave him until he promised to come to Gaza after 
sunset. When he arrived there, he made the sign of the cross on the bed and on her ill 
children and called upon the wondrous name of Jesus. Then, the children started sweating 
all at once and then when they recovered they recognized their mother, and everyone kissed 
the saint’s hands in gratitude.”

Jesus Prayer? 
The story of the anonymous Russian pilgrim who longed to enjoy the Jesus  Prayer was 
first published in Russia in 1865, and translated into several languages including Arabic .297

94 
O Lord, see the feebleness of my soul, and send down Your grace to help me, that I 
may glorify Your name. 
O Lord, sprinkle into my heart the dew of Your grace. 
O Lord, receive me in penitence and forsake me not. 
O Lord, give me tears and remembrance of death, and contrition. 
O Lord, give me humility, chastity, and obedience. 
O Lord, give me patience, magnanimity, and meekness. 
O Lord, let Your will be done in me, sinner, through the intercessions and prayers of the 
pure Virgin Saint Mary and all Your saints, for blessed are You unto the ages. Amen.294 
962. Did St. Ephrem the Syrian use arrow prayers?  
The Nisibene Hymns ( Carmina Nisiben a) of St. Ephrem the Syrian 295 are 
characterized by having harmonious, rhythmic stanzas that are suitable for church 
gatherings. Usually, each stanza is followed by a refrain that is sung with a special melody 
and can be prayed by anyone during their communal as well as personal worshi p, to help 
him offer his prayers with a spirit of hope and joy, and feel the divine presence. These are 
similar to arrow prayers or the Jesus Prayer, in that they represent a cry to God. 
963. Does the Paradise of the Fathers refer to the Jesus Prayer? 
The Paradise of the Fathers mentions some practical exercises that relate to the practice 
of the Jesus Prayer under the heading of “Calling on the name of the Lord Jesus.” 296 Here 
are some examples:  
“An elder said: ‘For in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godh ead bodily,  as the 
Apostle says (Col. 2:9). Therefore, we can never accept the thought of the defiled demons 
who claim that by calling on the name of Jesus we are not calling the Father or the Holy 
Spirit. For they do so out of their craftiness, denying us the uttera nce of the sweet name of 
our Lord Jesus Christ because they know that without this name there is no salvation as St. 
Peter the Apostle says: ‘There is no other name under heaven given among men by which 
we must be saved’  (Acts 4:12). We have no doubt whats oever that by calling on the name 
of our Lord Jesus, we are also calling the Father and the Holy Spirit; for we can never 
accept any division in the Godhead and we know that our Lord Jesus is the Mediator 
 
294 Twenty-four prayers — a prayer for each hour — traditionally ascribed to St. John Chrysostom. 
295 See NPNF II/13:165ff. 
296 See the Arabic extended version of the Paradise of the Fathers published by the Monastery of St. 
Macarius.

records.question: Why does God sometimes delay answering our prayers?
records.answer:
God sometimes delays answering our prayers for several reasons that reflect His wisdom and love for humanity. One significant reason is that such delays can increase our zeal and desire to approach Him. St. Basil the Great explains that God may delay an answer to help us appreciate the gift we are seeking, emphasizing that "that which a person receives with great effort, he strives to protect" [1]. This suggests that when we wait for something, we may value it more deeply once we receive it.

Additionally, St. Augustine points out that delays can teach us the value of persistence in prayer. He uses the example of the unjust judge from Luke 18, noting that if even an unjust judge can be moved by persistent requests, how much more will God, who is loving and just, respond to our prayers? Augustine asserts that God may not answer immediately to show us the importance of our requests and to encourage us not to lose heart in our supplications [1][2].

Moreover, there are times when our requests may not align with what is truly good for us. Abba Isaac indicates that sometimes we ask for things that are opposed to our salvation, and in such cases, God, in His wisdom, may choose to deny those requests for our ultimate benefit [7]. This aligns with the understanding that God's perspective on what is good for us is far greater than our own.

In summary, God's delays in answering prayers can serve to deepen our faith, teach us persistence, and ensure that our requests align with His divine wisdom and love for our well-being.

“Abba Macarius was asked, ‘How should one pray? ’ The old man said, ‘There is no 
need at all to make long discourses; it is enough to stretch out one ’s hands and s ay, “Lord, 
as you will, and as you know, have mercy. ” And if the conflict grows fiercer say, “Lord, 
help!” He knows very well what we need and he shews us his mercy.’”46  
Abba Isaac says, “For so far will one be heard and obtain an answer, as he believes that 
he is regarded by  God, and that God can grant it. For this saying of our Lord cannot be 
retracted: ‘Whatsoever you ask when you  pray, believe that you shall receive, and they 
shall come to you’ (Mark 11:24).”47  
St. John Cassian says, “He is quite certain that his prayers will not be answered. Who 
is this wretch? It is he who prays and does not believe that he will receive an answer.” 
899. What should you do if God answers your prayers for your brother or sister? 
St. John Climacus says, “Do not be puffed up if you have prayed for another and been 
heard, for it is his faith that has been strong and effective.”48 
900. Why does God sometimes delay answering our prayers, and why does He 
sometimes not answer them at all? 
St. Basil the Great says, “It may be that He delays answering a prayer so that your zeal 
and your desire to approach Him may be multiplied, and that you may appreciate the gift of 
God and guard it carefully when you have received it. That which a person  receives with 
great effort, he strives to protect, lest in losing it his labor will have been in vain.”49  
St. Augustine says, “He, who was not willing to give [the unjust judge  in Luke 18:2], 
gave what was asked, because the other did not faint in asking. How much more then shall 
that Good One give who exhorts us to ask, who is displeased if we ask not? But when at 
times He gives somewhat slowly, it is that He is showing us the value of His good things; 
not that He refuses them. Things which have been long desired, are obtained with the 
greater pleasure, whereas those which are given quickly, are held cheap.”50  
“Some things, indeed, we wish because we are in  Christ, and other things we desire 
because still in this world … Abiding, therefore, ourselves in Him, when His words abide 
in us we sh all ask what we will, and it shall be done unto us. For if we ask, and the doing

freedom of converse is born out of constant association with him.”43 
898. How can we offer prayer that is acceptable before God? 
The purpose of prayer is to keep the relationship between God and the person alive and 
effective. Therefore, we should consider the following when we pray: 
a. Trust in God who has complete love for humanity,  ability, wisdom, and knowledge 
(cf. Col. 2:2; Eccl. 8:17).  
b. Pray for the will of God in every matter, for He is the Pantocrator : “Thy will be 
done” (Matt. 6:10). 
c. Offer prayer from a heart that is unsoiled and pure.  
d. Begin every prayer with thanksgiving for the things that  God has granted us, for 
there is n o gift  that is not increased  except that which is received  without 
thanksgiving, according to St. Isaac the Syrian. 
e. Believe in the verse that says , “Unless the lord builds the house, they labor in vain 
who built it” (Ps. 127:1). 
f. Acknowledge that divine grace works in synergy with human striving. The Lord 
saved the child Moses and at the same time He rewarded the two midwives for 
ignoring pharaoh’s evil decree (Ex. 1:20).  
St. Basil the Great says, “There are conditions for a prayer to be answered : it must be 
according to the will of God (Matt. 26:39); we must be steadfast and persistent (Luke 11:8); 
we must realize that God’s wants us to reform our conduct , which is much more important 
than answering our prayers (Isa . 1:15); we must  be aware of  our unworthiness of that for 
which we ask (1 Chron. 17:4) or the unworthiness of those for whom we pray (Jer. 14:11); 
and that sometimes the lack of an answer to prayer is preferable to it being answered (2 
Cor. 12:7) … If all these conditions are met, then t here is no doubt that God will answer 
our prayers.”44 
Abba Zeno says, “If a man wants God to hear his prayer quickly, then before he prays 
for anything else, even his own soul, when he stands and stretches out his hands towards 
God, he must pray with all his heart for his enemies. Through this action God will hear 
everything that he asks.”45  
 
43 St. Isaac of Nineveh, On Ascetical Life (PP 11).

45 Ward, Benedicta. The Sayings of the Desert Fathers: The Alphabetical Collection, trans., Benedicta Ward 
(Liturgical Press, 1984) Zeno 7: p. 65.

subject to corruption, we do not in any wise ‘answer’ our Creator, seeing that whereas

that it is a creature, has it inherent in itself to sink down below itself, but man has obtained 
it from his Creator, that he should both be caught above himself by contemplation, and held

vessels, but is not satisfied until the time of the wedding comes and she is made one with 
him, so the soul, when it is engaged as a bride to the heavenly Bridegroom, receives as an

904. Why do we pray? Does God not know what we need? 
St. Basil the Great  says, “He undoubtedly knows  [what we need]  and He gives us 
abundantly all temporal things even before we ask. However, we should first ask for the 
things that are profitable and for the kingdom of heaven, and thereafter we receive what we 
desire; but let us ask patiently and faithfully, ask for wh at is good for us, and let us not 
hinder our prayers by disobeying our consciences.”84 
905. Are communal prayers necessary?  
The believer feels that he is in communion with his brothers and sisters in prayer even 
in his private room, and thus he prays for all and asks for their prayers on his behalf. St. 
Basil wrote to one of the widows , “ be mindful of  God and have the fear of Him in your 
heart, and invite all to a union with you in your prayers. For great is the assistance of those 
who are able to move God.”85  
St. Ambrose says, “ For if according to the Lord ’s saying , that that which two shall 
have agreed upon on earth concerning anything which they shall ask, shall be done for 
them, as He says, by My Father, Who is in heaven, for: ‘Where two or three are gathered 
together in My Name, there am I in the midst of them’ (Matt. 18:19) … how much less, 
where the full congregation is gathered in the Name of the Lord. Where the demand of all is 
unanimous, ought we to doubt that the Lord Jesus is there as the Author of that desire, and 
the Hearer of the petition.”86  
“Believe, then, that the Lord Jesus is present at the invocation of the  priest, Who 
said: ‘For where two or three are , there I am also’ (Matt. 18:20). How much where 
the Church is, and where His Mysteries are, does He vouchsafe to impart His presence!”87 
906. Is it helpful to prolong prayer? 
St. Augustine says, “In view of this, it is not reprehensible or useless to pray at length 
when one is free, that is, when the obligations of other good and necessary works do not 
prevent us, although even in those, as I said, we must always pray by that desire of the 
heart.”88 
907. What does the Lord Christ mean by saying, “ask … seek … knock” (Luke 11:9)? 
St. Augustine says, “In order that these three things —viz. asking, seeking, knocking—
may be made clear, let us suppose, for example , the case of one weak in his limbs, who

89 
956. Does prayer without ceasing justify a neglect of performing actions? 
St. Mark the Ascetic says, “Whoever wants to reach ‘the measure of the stature of the 
fullness of Christ’ (Eph. 4:13) must not prefer any w ork over prayer, yet he should still 
undertake other work lest be in need … He must not refrain from doing the essential duties 
required by  divine law on the excuse that he is devoting himself to  prayer. He should 
distinguish between prayer and work, obeying the divine law without question [i.e., do both 
together].” 
957. How can one deal with distracting thoughts that disturb prayer? 
First: Cling to the Lord.  St. Isaac the Syrian  says, “Sit before His face all your time, 
thinking of Him and recollecting Him in your heart, lest, seeing Him only after long you 
should not lack freedom of speech with Him on account of bashfulness. A high degree of 
freedom of speech is born from consta nt intercourse. Constant intercourse with men is of a 
bodily nature; that with God is psychic meditation and offerings in prayers … For the heart 
of those who seek the Lord rejoices. Seek the Lord, you sinners and be strengthened in 
hope in your thoughts. Seek His face by repentance at all times and you will be sanctified 
by the holiness of His face and you will be purified from your unrighteousness. Speed unto 
the Lord, you unrighteous, the Lord who forgives unrighteousness and effaces sins.”290 
Second: Pray with the spirit of hope.  St. Augustine says , “I seem to feel that for this 
reason he calls God gracious, because He bears with those failings of ours, and yet expects 
prayer from us, in order to make us perfect: and when we have given it to Him, He recei ves 
it gratefully, and listens to it, and does not remember those many prayers which we pour 
out unthinkingly, and accepts the one which we can scarcely find. For what man is there, 
my brethren, who, on being addressed by his friend, when he wishes to answ er his address, 
sees his friend turn away from him and speak to another, who is there who would bear this? 
Or if you appeal to a judge, and set him up to hear you, and all at once, while you are 
speaking to him, pass from him, and begin to converse with yo ur friend, who would endure 
this? Yet God endures the hearts of so many persons who pray and think of different things 
… What then? Must we despair of mankind, and say that every man is already condemned 
into whose prayers any wandering thoughts have crept and interrupted them? If we say this, 
my brethren, I know not what hope remains. Therefore because there is some hope before 
God, because His mercy is great, let us say unto Him, ‘For unto You, O Lord, have I lifted 
up my soul’ [Ps. 86:4]. And how have I lifted it up? As I could, as You gave me strength, 
as I could catch it when it fled away. … From infirmity I sink: heal me, and I shall stand: 
strengthen me, and I shall be strong. But until You do this, bear with me.”291

Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen, 1923) 5 (73): p. 50 amended. 
291 St. Augustine of Hippo, Expositions on the Book of Psalms 86.7 (NPNF I/8:412) amended.

that prayer which He taught, and in which we say,  Our Father,  who art in  heaven 
(Matt. 6:9). Let us only not fall away from the words and meaning of this  prayer in our 
petitions, and whatever we ask, it shall be done unto us … But when His words abide only 
in the memory, and have no place in the life, the branch is not to be accounted as in the 
vine, because it draws not its life from the root.”51 
Abba Isaac, the disciple of St. Anthony,  says, “We sometimes ask for things opposed 
to our salvation and that we are most providentially refused our requests by Him who sees 
what is good for us with greater right and  truth than we can. And it is clear that this also 
happened to the teacher of the  Gentiles when he  prayed that the messenger of  Satan who 
had been for his good allowed by the Lord ’s will to buffet him, might be removed, 
saying: ‘For which I besought the Lord thrice that he might depart from me. And He said to 
me, My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness ’ (2 Cor. 12:8–
9).”52  
Pope Gregory the Great  says, “why is it that Paul three times besought the Lord and 
did not merit to be heard, but was told: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made 
perfect in weakness  (2 Cor. 12:9). Did the great preacher not ask in the name of the Son? 
Then why didn’t he r eceive what he asked? … The Son’s name is Jesus. Jesus means 
‘saviour’ or ‘saving.’ One who asks in the Saviour’s name asks what pertains to actual 
salvation. If what he asks for is not for his good he is not asking the Father in Jesus’ name. 
Hence the Lord says to his apostles while they were still weak, Up to now you have asked 
nothing in my name  (John 16:24) … That is the reason too why Paul was not heard. If he 
had been freed from temptation it would not have been of help to his salvation … consider 
your requests, I beseech you, and see if you are asking in the name of Jesus, if you are 
asking for the joys of eternal salvation … Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and 
all these things will be given you as well (Matt. 6:33).”53 
901.  What are the effects of prayer? 
First: The soul is inflamed with the love of God. St. Basil the Great says, “Prayers, too, 
following reading, take hold upon a fresher and more vigorous soul already stirred to a 
longing for God. And prayer which imprints in the soul a clear conception of God is an 
excellent thing. This abiding of God in our memory is the indwelling of God.  Thus we

records.question: What does the word catechism mean?
records.answer:
The term "catechism" originates from the Greek word that means a summary of religious teaching. It is presented either orally or in written form, typically structured as a series of questions and answers. This method serves to convey the principles and foundations of Christian teachings and values, and it has been utilized since the apostolic age, as noted in the Gospel of Luke (1:4) [1].

The primary purpose of catechism is to facilitate an understanding of the Christian faith, ultimately aiming for a deeper knowledge of God and His work of salvation. This understanding is not merely intellectual; it involves a relationship with God that is nurtured through divine grace. Early Church Fathers, such as St. Clement of Alexandria, emphasized that true knowledge comes from a sanctified mind, contrasting it with the Gnostic belief that salvation is achieved solely through rational knowledge [1]. 

Moreover, catechism is designed to be engaging and infused with love, rather than a dry recitation of rules. St. John Chrysostom highlighted that the essence of teaching should be rooted in love, suggesting that even a small act of love is more valuable than extensive discussions devoid of it [1]. Thus, catechism aims to inspire joy and humility in the lives of believers, encouraging them to live out their faith actively and lovingly in all aspects of life [1][7].

Book 1: Introduction to the Coptic Catechism 
5 
1 
(a) Catechism 
1. What does the word catechism mean? 
The word catechism is a Greek word that means a summary of religious teaching, 
presented either orally or through a book, of the principles and foundations of Christian 
teachings and values, generally in the form of questions and answers.2 This Greek word has 
been used since the apostolic age (Luke 1:4). Early Church Fathers such as St. Cyril of 
Jerusalem and St. Gregory of Nyssa  addressed catechumens through articles or lectures 
referred to as Catechetical Lectures. 
2. What is the purpose of a catechism (teaching through questions and answers)? 
First: to present an understanding of the faith, with the goal of knowing God and 
His work of salvation. St. Clement of Alexandria (second century) differentiated between 
the knowledge of the Gnostic s, who believed that man can only be saved through his own 
rational knowledge; and the knowledge that is based on the sanctification of the mind through 
the divine grace of God, submitting to faithfully learn about God and build a relationship 
with Him, and asking for His grace in our lives. As St. Jude the apostle mentions “contend 
earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3) and St. Peter, 
“receiving the end of your faith — the salvation of your souls” (1 Pet. 1:9). St.  Paul also 
invites us to faith, saying “but without faith, it is impossible to please Him, for he who comes 
to God must believe that He is a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him” (Heb. 11:6). And 
“For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in G od” (Col. 3:3). We therefore escape 
from the corruption that is in the world on account of lust (2 Pet. 1:4). St. Paul the apostle 
said, “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you 
both to will and to do for His good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13), so that we may enjoy the holy 
life by faith working through love (Gal. 5:6). 
Second: the principles of catechism are not based on a set of rules that are memorized 
dryly or in discussions bereft of the spirit of love. St. John Chrysostom says that the fruit 
of an ounce of love is better than that a ton of discussion. I hope that the effect of this book 
will be to spread the spirit of love and to invite the spirit of joy and humility to work in the 
lives of all the faithful all over the world, from the little children to the elderly. As the son of 
Sirach says, a believer does not cease from his labor till the last breath of his life. “Stand fast 
in your covenant and become familiar with it and grow old in the work of your 
commandments” (Sir. 11:18). 
 
2 Cf. https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/catechism

a. The Hearers: These were allowed to attend sermons and listen to some chapters from 
Scripture before the deacon asked them to leave.1317  
b. The Prostrates: These were entitled to attend the Liturgy of the Word and listen to 
the scripture readings, sermon, and a special prayer of the catechumens, 1318 which 
was part of the litanies prayed after the sermon; after which they received the laying 
on of hands for blessing while bowing down (i.e., while prostrate). 
c. Baptism Candidates: These were called the “enlightened” or those who are ready 
for baptism.  
The Church was not rigid and allowed catechumens in any stage to receive the baptism 
if they were in mortal danger, as St. Basil mentions in his letter to the bereaved wife of 
Arintheus, the Roman general whose wife arranged for him to be baptized just bef ore he 
died.1319 St. Epiphanius of Salamis says that a catechumen who believes in the resurrection 
from the dead and has this hope is in his heart, should be baptized if he was in danger of 
death so that his hope may not be lost. In any case, the Great Lent was the period in which 
the catechumens were taught daily. Egeria the pilgrim says, “It is the custom here for those 
who want to get baptized to come every day during the Great Lent.”  
During times of fasting, St. Cyril of Jerusalem says, “let the men w hen sitting have a 
useful book; and let one read, and another listen: and if there be no book, let one pray, and 
another speak something useful. And again let the party of young women sit together in like 
manner, either singing or reading quietly, so that their lips speak, but others’ ears catch not 
the sound … And let the married woman also follow the same example and pray; and let her 
lips move, but her voice be unheard, that a Samuel may come, and your barren soul give birth 
to the salvation of God who h as heard your prayer; for this is the interpretation of the name 
Samuel.”1320

deeds. Origen says, “Every disciple of Christ is a rock, by which the church currently being

The Basic Principles of Catechism 
5. What are the basic principles of catechism in the Coptic Orthodox Church?  
It is fitting for us as believers to benefit from the experience of our fathers through the 
stages of catechism over the centuries, that we may live with a spiritual, living, Biblical 
mindset in every aspect of our lives; whether in our study of the Holy B ible, our practice of 
the truly evangelical life, or in our daily conduct; even our eating and drinking, our worship 
in the spirit of truth, and our service for every person we meet, even if we do not know them 
personally, and in our conversations with believers and nonbelievers.  
St. Clement of Alexandria  describes the life of the Christian believer in his book The 
Instructor (Paedagogus). He explains that our faith in Christ must be translated into action. 
We live in Christ Jesus when we walk alongside the elderly whose movement is slow and 
when we walk alongside the young who are quick in their movements; in our smile and our 
refraining from inappropriate laughter; in our observance of table manners as those in the 
conscious presence of God; i n our sleep …so the believer lives as an ambassador of Christ 
in all matters, whether they seem important or trivial. And he does all this without either the 
literalism that kills or tedious routine.23 
In all of this, there are two important considerations: our hearts should be inflamed with 
love for the Lord Christ while we await His swift coming on the clouds to take us into His 
heavenly bridal chamber; and we should also be constantly occupied with the salvation of 
the whole world, even of those who have  fallen into what we may deem serious crimes or 
impure sins! 
6. What are the most important practical principles of catechism?  
First: it is appropriate for us to present whatever we are able —together with our 
evangelist, St. Mark the Apostle—of the Lord of Glory, who is the heavenly Physician ; 
Savior of souls; healer of the soul, intellect, emotions, senses, and every activity of the body.  
I am reminded of someone who made every effort for a long time to attract a friend to the 
Gospel of Christ. The frien d finally agreed to go to church to listen to a famous preacher. 
That evening, the church’s priest called him to ask about the sermon he had attended. His 
response was: “I could barely tolerate listening to him for ten minutes and I left because I 
was internally resenting the world and its hardships. This preacher incessantly attacked me, 
 
23 I hope, if God wills, to present the approach of St. Clement of Alexandria—one of the pillars of the School 
of Alexandria—in The Life in Christ Jesus.

records.question: Who was St. Abanoub el-Nehissy?
records.answer:
St. Abanoub el-Nehissy was a young martyr from Nehissah, a village in the city of Talkha, who lived during the 4th century. He was raised by pious parents who instilled in him strong Christian values and a love for God and the Holy Bible. Tragically, he lost both parents at the tender age of 12, which left him deeply sorrowful, earning him the nickname "the lamented boy" due to his prolonged grief over their loss. This emotional vulnerability illustrates the human experience of loss, even among those of strong faith, as seen in the examples of St. Paul and Abraham, who also faced personal struggles despite their faith [1].

After his parents' death, Abanoub was inspired by a sermon he heard in church about enduring suffering for the sake of faith. This led him to seek God's guidance through prayer, and he felt compelled to walk to the city of Semenood, desiring to earn a heavenly crown for his faith [1]. His journey marked the beginning of his commitment to live out his Christian beliefs, which ultimately led him to face persecution.

Abanoub's faith was tested when he was captured and tortured by the governor of Atrib. Despite enduring severe tortures, including being put in boiling oil and having his eyes blinded, he remained steadfast in his faith. Throughout his trials, he was reportedly aided by Archangel Michael, who healed him and inspired many witnesses to convert to Christianity, some of whom also became martyrs [2]. His unwavering commitment to Christ and his miraculous acts, such as healing a possessed woman, further solidified his legacy as a martyr.

Eventually, Abanoub was sent to Alexandria, where he continued to confess his faith despite facing more tortures. He was ultimately beheaded for his beliefs, and his body was buried in his hometown of Nehissah. The church commemorates his martyrdom on the 24th of Abib [2]. His story serves as a powerful testament to the strength of faith in the face of suffering and the transformative power of God's grace.

ABANOUB EL-NEHISSY 
(The martyr) 
St. Abanoub was born in Nehissah, in the city of Talkha in the 4th Century. 
His parents were pious loving parents who raised him with Christian values 
and planted in him the love for God and the Holy Bible. He was only 12 years 
of age when both his parents departed to Paradise. Missing his parents was so 
devastating to the young Abanoub, that he was called the lamented boy for he 
was sorrowful for so long. Some might ask wonder how could he manage to 
withstand all the sufferings that he encountered later on and yet could not resist 
the loss of his parents. 
It is true that despite our faith in heavenly life, it will not strip us from our 
human feelings; instead, it would sanctify them. We can see an illustration of 
that in the presence of St. Paul, who wrote about the door being opened for 
evangelism in Troas, and yet he could not find peace in his soul, for he could 
not find his friend Titus, so he left the city. "Furthermore, when I came to Troas 
to [preach] Christ's gospel, and a door was opened to me by the Lord, I had no 
rest in my spirit, because I did not find Titus, my brother, but taking my leave 
of them, I departed for Macedonia” (2 Cor. 2:12-13). This situation shows the 
vulnerability of human nature, and God may allow those weaknesses to prevent 
us from boasting. Another example of weakness was with our  great father 
Abraham, who said that his wife Sarah was his sister for fear that the king 
might kill him to take her for a wife (Gen. 20:2). Also, our beloved St. Mark, 
who left Paul and Barnabas and caused them to have an argument and ended 
up separating from each other (Acts 13:3), and St. Peter, who was leaving 
Rome for fear of persecution and Jesus appeared to him too and kindly 
corrected him. Therefore, we should not be troubled when we show weakness 
despite the grace given to us, for it is beneficial in keeping us humble and 
urging us to ask God to work in us and with us. 
In the village's church: 
One day, Abanoub went to the church and heard the priest during the sermon 
encouraging the congregation to endure with joy the suffering and persecution 
they were getting for their faith. After the Holy Communion, the young 
Abanoub went home, while the priest’s words still ringing in his ears.  
At home, he knelt to pray, asking for God ’s guidance. Then, he stood up 
and started walking towards the city of Semeno od (about 12 miles away), 
while rejoicing in the spirit and desiring to have the heavenly crown. 
In Semenood:

passages.text:
35 
 
At this point, the governor asked Abanoub to pray for him so that he and his 
soldiers could be healed. Abanoub told him that God would heal them in Atrib. 
When they got there, Abanoub prayed for the governor and treated him in the 
Lord’s name in the presence of Atrib ’s governor. This miracle caused many 
pagans to believe in the Lord, and some were martyred. 
In Atrib (Banha) 
Regardless, the governor of Atrib tortured Abanoub with all kinds of torture 
methods and put him in boiling oil and cut up his feet and hands and b linded 
his eyes with hot rods. During all these trials, God did not leave Abanoub, but 
He always sent Archangel Michael to heal him. Many witnesses became 
Christians and gladly became martyrs, from watching the young Abanoub 
enduring all that suffering and still praising his God. 
In Alexandria 
After the governor of Atrib saw the multitude of people accepting 
Abanoub's faith, he tied him up with reliable chains and sent him to Alexandria. 
There, he met a woman who had an evil spirit, and he forced the spirit  out of 
her, and she became Christian. Consequently, the soldiers killed her because 
she said that she believed in Christ.  
Abanoub continued to confess his faith in our Lord Jesus before the 
governor Arminius of Alexandria who also tortured him and put him in a room 
filled with snakes and serpents and the Archangel Michael got him out of it, 
and the snakes followed him, and one of them coiled itself around the 
governor's neck. He cried out to Abanoub, and he saved him, which caused 
many to believe and become martyrs.  
Abanoub suffered more tortures and was finally beheaded outside the city 
on a high rock where he stood to pray, asking God to forgive him and to accept 
his soul.  
St. Julius El-Akfahsy took his body and buried him in his town Nehissah, 
and wrote his story. His body was moved from Nehissah to Semenood, and the 
church celebrates his martyrdom on the 24th of Abib. 
 
ABANOUB, THE CONFESSOR, ST. 
The word ‘Abanoub’ is derived from the Coptic word ‘Pi-Noub’ meaning 
(gold). This saint was a virtuous mon k in one of the monasteries of Upper 
Egypt in the days of Diocletian, who tortured and shed the blood of 80 martyrs 
in a single day. 
It so happened when the name of St. Abanoub was mentioned before 
Arianius, the governor of Ansena, that the governor called him and asked him 
to worship the idols. The saint answered, saying: “How can I forsake my Lord

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 52
passages.text:
52 
 
the entire night in the church, attending the Holy Liturgy in the early morning, 
partaking of the Holy Communion, and then he would go back to his cave. 
His Scribing: 
The saint was gifted with beautiful handwriting in both Coptic and Arabic 
languages. He preoccupied himself with copying so many ancient books. He 
also authored so many new books. Besides, he cared for binding the books and 
making leather gir dles and Eskeems. In addition to all those preoccupations 
and seclusion, he was the father of confession for all the monks of the 
‘Baramus’ monastery. 
Finally, Fr. ‘Abd-el-Mesih El-Masoudy’ reposed in peace on the 11th of Tout 
1621 AM (21 December 1905), at the age of 88 years. He was a monk for 71 
years in the monasteries of ‘Moharraq,’ ‘Baramus’ and in seclusion. 
[The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 5, p. 106] 
 
ABD-JESUS THE BISHOP AND HIS COMPANIONS, SS. 
(The martyrs) 
In the days of the king of Persia ‘Shapur II’ (309-379 AD), around the year 
361 AD, five who carried the same name “Abd-jesus’ (Hebed-Jesus) were 
martyred: one of them was a bishop, three priests, a deacon and a monk. 
Bishop ‘Abdjesus,’ along with another bishop called ‘Abdas’ and a third 
bishop named ‘Dausas,’ were led captives to the area of ‘Zabde,’ where they 
were martyred. 
[A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. II, p. 23] 
 
ABDON AND SENNEN, SS. 
(The martyrs) 
Two Persian Christians who were martyred in the days of Emperor ‘Decius’ 
(249-251 AD). Their biography could be found under the letter “S." 
 
ABE-FAM (Bifam/Phoebammon) EL-TAHAWY 
(The martyr) 
Pagan parents raised this saint in the city of ‘Taha’ in Upper Egypt. When 
he was 12 years old, his father gave many gifts to the prince to let his son join 
the army. Abe -Fam (Bifam/Phoebammon) eventually became a prominent 
officer, known for his love of justice and his defense of the oppressed and the

passages.text:
36 
 
Jesus Christ, and worship the idols made of stone?! ” Therefore, he tortured 
him severely, and then he sent him to the five western cities (the Pentapolis), 
where he was imprisoned for as long as seven years until Diocletian perished. 
When the righteous Emperor Constantine reigned, he gave his command to set 
free all those Christians who were in prisons and to bring them forth to him to 
have their blessing. He specified that in case it is difficult to bring them all, to 
bring only the prominent ones among them, such as ‘Zacharias Al-Ahnasy,’ 
Maximianus of Fayum, Agabius of ‘Dakhnin,’ and Abanoub of ‘Balaos.' The 
saints came out of their imprisonments, singing praises to God.  
At that time, St. Abanoub, the confessor, returned from ‘Pentapolis’ and 
dwelt on a mountain close to his homeland. When the Emperor’s envoy came, 
they took him on a boat to Ansena, where he encountered the believers, and 
the bishops ordained h im as a priest. And, it so happened that, while he was 
uttering: “The Holies are for the holy, ” that he saw the Lord Christ 
transfiguring in the church with His exalted glory.  
The Emperor’s envoy traveled together with 72 saints and put every two of 
them in a carriage, and while passing through one of the cities, where there 
was a nunnery of virgins, 700 of them came out singing hymns before them.  
When they reached the capital, the king sought from them to change their 
worn-out clothes to expensive new on es, but they declined his offer. He then 
kissed their wounds, honored them, and offered them precious gifts, which 
they also refused, except for some curtains and vessels for their churches, to 
which they returned, and St. Abanoub returned to his monastery. 
Finally, after fulfilling his strife, he reposed in peace. 
[Synaxarion, 23 Paona] 
 
ABASKHIRON AL-QUALINI 
(The martyr) 
The saint ’s name is derived from two words: The word ‘Abba’ means 
(Father) and the word ‘Skhiron,’ ‘Eskhirus,’ or ‘Eskaros,’ which means (the 
Strong). He was born in the town of ‘Qualin’ in the governorate of ‘Kafr El-
Sheikh’ in the Nile delta. He was a brave and beloved soldier, famous and 
appreciated by his leaders and fellow soldiers in the regiment that was camped 
in ‘Atrib’ (Benha). 
His position from the decree of Diocletian: 
Emperor Diocletian issued an order, mandating the sacrifice to idols by 
everybody all over his empire. When this decree was declared before the 
regiment’s soldiers, ‘Abaskhiron’ refused totally to obey. Then, the governor

Besides, his brother ‘Aba-Bishai’ was martyred on the first day of the 
‘Nasie’ (The little month).  
 [The Synaxarion: 29 Paona] 
 
ABAHOR, THE MONK, ST. 
This father from ‘Abraht’ in the area of the ‘Ashmonein,’ was an elect monk 
who surpassed many saints in his worship. Loving solitude and living alone in 
the wilderness, he was envied by the devil who appeared to him and said: “In 
the wilderness, you can overcome me because you are there alone, but I 
challenge you if you are brave, go to Alexandria." He instantly set forth to 
Alexandria, where he stayed sometimes serving the prisoners. 
It so happened that some horses were galloping in midtown, and one of 
them knocked down a little kid who instantly died. As St. Abahor was standing 
at the place where that incident took place, the devil provoked some people 
around to shout aloud, claiming that it was the old monk who killed him. When 
many started to revile and to scoff him, St. Abahor calmly took the kid to his 
bosom, prayed in his heart t o the Lord Christ, and then made the sign of the 
cross on him. The kid came back to life, and he gave him to his parents. Those 
around him glorified God and started to make it up to the old monk, who, 
fearing from the vainglory, he fled to the wilderness, where he dwelt for days 
in a monastery. 
When it was time for him to depart from this world, he saw a group of saints 
calling him to join them, for which he greatly rejoiced, became joyful, called 
his spiritual disciples to inform them that he will soon depart to the Lord Christ, 
and provided them with his last commandment. Hearing that, they much 
grieved that they will be orphans after his departure. He felt sick for a little 
while, and then he delivered his soul in the Lord’s hand. 
 [The Synaxarion: 2 Kiahk] 
 
ABAHOR 
(The martyr) 
He was born in ‘Seriakos’ to a father who was a blacksmith. Deciding to die 
a martyr, he set forth to ‘Al-Farma’ (nowadays: ‘Port Said ’), where he 
confessed the Lord Christ before its governor. The governor tortured him but 
much astonished at how the Lord came to comfort him and heal his wounds. 
Therefore, the governor, together with his entire household, proclaimed their 
faith in the Lord Christ. Accordingly, they were martyred by the hands of the

362 
 
youth of both genders . He also supported hundreds of advanced youth to 
complete their higher education. Then he got occupied with printing the 
lessons of Sunday schools and publishing the Ecclesiastical books. 
• In the year 1938, he contributed to establishing the “ Bookstore of el-
MaĥAbba” to publish and distribute all kinds of Coptic publications,  
through which he issued “The Message of el-MaĥAbbah,” and then “The 
Calendar of el-MaĥAbbah.” 
• Continuing on his spiritual strife , he established “The House of e l-
MaĥAbbah” in the year 1941 . He  annexed it by setting the church of 
Archangel Michael and St. Shenouda, which was dedicated on the 21 st of 
September 1957. 
• As though work led to more energy, so he established a building to embrace 
all the diverse activities of the Society of el-MaĥAbbah, then the House of 
el-MaĥAbbah in the year 1960. And adorned the building by an altar in the 
name of St. Anba Abram, which eventually turned into a church.  
• With his advanced age, his activity increased , and he set the foundation of 
a nursery and a house for the out -of-town female students, facing the 
building of the Society of el-MaĥAbbah on Jazerit Badran street. 
When the 116th Pope of Alexandria, St. Kyrillos VI (Cyril VI: 1959-1971) 
decided to establish a vast Cathedral in the name of St. Mark the Apostle on 
the land of Anba Roweis, the pope formed a committee to collect donations for 
such an enormous enterprise. He chose archon Younan Nakhla as one of its 
members. In the year 1972, the country president Anwar Sadat (1970 -1981) 
bestowed on him the highest medal of Imtiaz (excellence) of the first grade . 
And, the governor of Cairo gave him a letter of appreciation on the day of 
Social Labor as an appreciation of his endless strife. After such shining 
conflict, he departed Paradise to enjoy the company of the Saints in the 1970s. 
     [The Faithful Synaxarion: 24 Toba] 
 
YOUNAN, THE MONK, ST. 
Cf. St. Jonah (Younan), the Monk. 
 
YOUSEF ABU-DAQN EL-MANUFI 
Yousef (Joseph) Abu-Daqn el-Manufi was one of the great Coptic archons 
in the 17 th century. A contemporary of the 101 st Pope of Alexandria, Abba 
Marcos VI’ (1646-1656). He authored a book entitled “ The True History of 
the Copts in Libya, Nubia, and Ethiopia.” In this book, he gave some details 
about the social and spiritual conditions  of those Copts  as well as their

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 50
passages.text:
50 
 
who granted his parents another son, and they called him ‘Hanna.' 
In the year 1914, ‘Samaan’ set forth to Abba Macarius monastery in the 
‘Scetis’ wilderness, where he became a monk by the name of ‘Abd-el-Mesih.' 
There, he was attached to Fr. ‘Abd-el-Mesih Salib El -Massoudy’ of the 
‘Baramus’ monastery and his brother Fr. ‘Yacob.' On hearing about the virtues 
of this saint, Fr. ‘Abd-el-Mesih El-Macary’; the 113th Pope of Alexandria Abba 
‘Yoannes XIX’ (1928-1942) planned to ordain him as a bishop. However, as 
the saint did not want to be raised to that rank, he pretended to be crazy and 
half-wit that the pope had to expel him from the papal residence. From that 
time on, he kept on that pretense, whenever he intended to escape from any 
vainglory. Fr. ‘Abd-el-Mesih Salib El -Massoudy’ counseled him to leave the 
monastery and to keep on following the same behavior. Therefore, he often 
pretended that he wanted to get married.  After he left the monastery, he lived 
in the village of ‘El-Manahra’ in his home district of ‘Matai’ in ‘El-Minya.' 
Therefore, he acquired the new title ‘El-Manahry.' 
His Worship: 
Nobody knows about his prayers, but he used to live in seclusion praying in 
his cell for periods extending to several weeks. He used to tie a rope to the 
ceiling of his cell and tie its other end around his waist to pull him up in case 
he would fall asleep while praying. He memorized all the praises and the 
church hymns by heart. He ate only once every day at sunset.  
He always gave alms generously to the needy, yet in his own crazy and half-
wit ways. He never had two mantles at the same time, and he lived in a cell 
built with mud bricks and not painted from the inside. In that manner, he gave 
a great example of monastic life. 
God honored him by the gift of performing miracles. And spiritually, he 
reached the rank of the hermits, as testified by the 116th Pope St. ‘Kyrillos VI’ 
(1959-1971). Besides, this saint has prophesied in advance about the ordination 
of Fr. ‘Mina El-Motawahid’ (St. ‘Kyrillos VI’) as a pope over the See of St. 
Mark. 
He finally reposed in peace on the morning of the Great feast of the 
Resurrection (the Easter) on the 6 th of Baramouda 1679 AM (14 April 1963). 
Moreover, since the Palm Sunday, before he reposed, the saint kept saying, “I 
shall be crowned and rejoice the day of the Feast. ” However, at the time, 
nobody paid attention to that statement, because it was also taken lightly as 
one of his usual crazy way of talking. 
[Abba Mena, bishop of Girga: The Biography of a Contemporary Saint: Fr. Abd -
el-Mesih St. Macar]

that if he wanted to be healed , he should promise God to forsake the 
priesthood for the rest of his life and to repent regretting his horrible 
behavior. As the priest did promise, the saint came out to pray for him, until 
he was wholly healed of his sickness with true repentance. 
2- A man came to him with his son to get his blessing. But, it happened that 
the son fell from the mountain and died. The father carried him to the cave 
of the saint, placed him in front of the entrance, and without telling the saint 
about what happened, he asked him to bless him. The saint made the sign 
of the cross on the boy, and said to him, “Get up, go to your father, and hold 
his hand.” So the boy did. In great joy, the father cast himself on the ground 
before the saint, thanking him and glorifying God who pe rforms miracles 
through His saints. 
3- Getting to know the day of his repose, he asked the priest to come over to 
perform the Holy Eucharist. He had communion standing on his swollen 
feet, bid farewell from the brethren, blessed them, sought their blessing, 
prayed, and delivered his soul in the hands of the Lord on 25 Amshir. 
His Monastery in Delga: 
A monastery was built in his name close to ‘Beni Khaled, a village of 
‘Delga’ about 20 kilometers south of the province of El-Ashmonein. 
[Nabil Selim: Monasteries of the Fathers (9): St. Epiphanius (Abu Fana) on Mount 
Delga; an annex of his book on ‘The Monasteries of the Fathers (8) on SS Bishai 
and Basentaos of the Tod] 
 
ABU SAAD MANSOUR 
He was among the 11th century Copts. His name was ‘Ebn-Abu- Al-Yomn.' 
He was an eloquent writer and a courageous man. He became a minister in the 
days of Calipha El-Mostanser; but had to quit when the Turkish soldiers sought 
their wages, and there was not enough money in the treasury to fulfill their 
requests. But when their leader  ‘Naser Al -Dawlah’ rebelled against the 
Calipha, then ‘Abu-Saad,’ supported by pro-Calipha regiment, bravely fought 
against him and defeated him. His loyalty and courage had a massive effect on 
the Calipha, who loved him very much. 
[Fr. Manasseh Yohanna: History of the Coptic Church; 1983; p. 398] 
 
ABU SALEM AL-MALATY 
He was among the 18th century Copts. A Coptic physician, by the name of 
‘Abu-Salem El-Nasrany El-Jacoby El-Malaty.' It was claimed that he was not

passages.label: Encyclopedia of the Saints and Fathers of the Church, Volume 1, p. 77
passages.text:
77 
 
given to the poor” (Ps. 112:9). 
He was called ‘Mematy’ on account of that when a famine dwelt on Egypt 
in his time, he gave plenty of wheat to the poor; and when the little children, 
knowing of his love, used to beg him calling him by this name; he used to give 
them with compassion. 
[Fr. Manasseh Yohanna: History of the Coptic Church; 1983, p. 399]  
[Martyr Abu Nagaah the Great; cf. Yohanna Abu Nagaah – Synaxarion 19 
Baramouda] 
 
ABU EL-SAIID AL-KATEB 
He was the chief of the archives department in the Fatimid era (in the 11 th 
century). He renovated the church of ‘The Five and their Mother’ (St. Rifka), 
at ‘Manial Shiha,’ in Giza. 
 
ABU AL-TAYEB 
He was among the 11th century Copts. He worked as a Secretary of ‘Naser 
Al-Dawla,’ the leader of the Turkish regiment in the days of Calipha ‘El-
Mostansir.' At that time, the Turks rebelled against the Calipha. They spread 
corruption, robbed the monasteries in Egypt, and kidnaped Pope Christodolus 
seeking to get a ransom for him from the Copts. Abu El -Tayeb hastened and 
used his influence to set him free from their hands. 
[Martyr Abu El-Elah Fahd Ebn Ibrahim: Synaxarion 19 Baramouda] 
 
ABU AL-YOMN YOUSEF 
He was among the 13 th century Copts. His full name wa s ‘Abu-Al-Yomn 
Yousef Ebn Macroah Ebn Zanbour,’ and he was known as the ‘chief treasurer.' 
He worked as the treasurer of the storehouses of the Caliph. Moreover, because 
of his unusual honesty, he was given the responsibility for the collected taxes 
of the entire area of Lower Egypt. 
To express his thanks to God and his love for his brethren, he built a great 
monastery in ‘Tamoah’ in Giza in the name of the martyr ‘Abu-Sifein’ (St. 
Marcorius). He planted vast gardens around it; that the minister ‘Badr Al-
Gamali’ used to spend most of his free time relaxing there. 
 [Fr. Manasseh Yohanna: History of the Coptic Church; 1983; p. 398]

54 
 
 [Nabil Selim and Guirgis El-Meniawy: St. John the Herculean & the Three Saintly 
Abe-Fams, June 1966] 
 
ABE-FAM (Bifam/Phoebammon) OF AUSIM, ST. 
(The martyr) 
St. ‘Abe-Fam’ was born in ‘Ausim’ to a father by the name of Anastasius 
and a pious mother by the name of Susanna. They raised him on the spirit of 
piety, worship, and the love of the poor. When he was nine years old, his father 
sent him to a virtuous priest by the name of ‘Ausanius’ to explain to him the 
Holy Bible and the teachings of the Church. 
One day, while he was on his way to the priest accompanied by another boy, 
he met with a leprous who asked him for a donation. Stretching his hand to 
give him something, the leprous was instantly healed. All the people were 
astonished and felt that this boy would have a great future, that even the priest 
himself sought from the boy to bless him. On the same night, an angel of the 
Lord appeared to tell the priest what would happen to the boy. As for Abe-Fam, 
he increased in repentance before God, fasted every day until evening,  and 
turned his bedroom to a cell for worshipping God. 
The Lord Christ appears to him: 
Worshipping God with piety and faithfulness, the Lord Christ appeared to 
him, and with Him, St. Mary the Virgin, the Mother of God, and the Archangel 
Gabriel. The Lord told him that he would receive the crown of martyrdom. In 
the morning, he was seen with an illuminated face, and a sweet fragrance came 
out of his room. The saint told his friend ‘Tawadros’ what he has seen. Later 
on, ‘Tawadros’ became the bishop of Ausim a nd wrote the biography of the 
saint. 
His Love of Virginity: 
In the feast of the Virgin Mary, his parents made a banquet for the poor, as 
it was their custom every year. They asked him about his intention concerning 
marriage. He answered them: “I intend to remain a virgin until I stand before 
the throne of the Lord Christ my God,” and his parents kept silent. After a few 
days, his father passed away, and the son practiced the works of mercy he 
inherited from his father. 
The Vision had seen by Abba Serapion: 
A saintly hermit by the name of ‘Serapion’ had told ‘Tawadros’ about a night 
vision he saw concerning his friend ‘Abe-Fam.' In that vision, he saw an angel 
who carried him to ‘Ausim,’ and on its west side, he showed him ‘Satanael’

records.question: How did St. Moses the Black come to faith?
records.answer:
St. Moses the Black, originally known for his life of crime and violence, experienced a profound transformation that led him to faith in Christ. Initially, he was a notorious gangster who led a life of robbery and murder, becoming the head of a gang due to his imposing physical stature and strength. Despite his extreme evil, he had a flicker of faith; he would raise his eyes to the sun, believing it to be the true God, and sought a way to encounter the divine [3].

His journey to faith began when he heard a voice urging him to go to the wilderness to meet the monks of Scetis, known for their piety and spiritual strength. Driven by a desire for redemption, he approached St. Isidore, a monk who became his spiritual guide. Moses confessed his past sins and expressed his deep remorse, demonstrating a sincere desire to change his life. St. Isidore taught him about God and the importance of repentance, encouraging him to contemplate his life and the judgment to come [3][5].

Moses's commitment to his new path was evident when he publicly confessed his sins in the church, which marked a significant step in his spiritual journey. He was baptized by Abba Macarius the Great, who recognized his genuine repentance and desire to live a monastic life. Following his baptism, Moses dedicated himself to ascetic practices, striving to overcome his past through rigorous spiritual discipline [1][3][5].

His transformation was not without struggle; he faced intense spiritual battles against the temptations of his former life. However, with the guidance of his mentors and his own determination, he persevered, ultimately becoming a revered monk and later a priest. His life exemplified the power of repentance and the grace of God to transform even the most hardened hearts into vessels of His love and service [1][4][5].

MOSES, THE LIBYAN, ST. 
This saint was from Libya. He was so humble and compassionate all the 
time that God granted him the grace to perform the miracles of healing the 
sick. He once said: “When I was young, I lived in a monastery. There, it 
happened that eight monks dug a well, and seventy others built a wall around 
it, in the hope that they would get water from it. They dug it down to the 
depth of about twenty yards, but no water was found. They were very much 
grieved and intended to fill it up with dirt. However, by noontime, w hen 
Abba Pieour came over suddenly to the location of the well and was 
informed about what they were doing, he rebuked them saying: ‘Why did you 
despair, O you of little faith? ’ Then, he went down to the bottom of the well, 
and he prayed there. Afterward, he pushed an iron rod in the well bottom 
three times, saying: ‘O God of the saints, I pray, do not waste the effort of 
these men, but send them plenty of water.’ In a short while, the water erupted 
from the well and wetted everyone around.  
After praying a  thanksgiving prayer, Abba Pieour intended to go in his 
way. They tried to make him have a meal with them, but he said: ‘I have 
accomplished what I came here to do, I did not come here to eat.’”  
This was a good lesson for the brethren about faith and the trust in God.  
 [The Paradise of the Saints, p. 69]

Emperor Valens sought to hold a treaty with queen Mavia and her people, the 
queen accepted on one condition, that the Emperor would see to it that the 
Egyptian monk Moses would go to Alexandria to be ordained as a bishop by 
the patriarch there. Although the queen was not yet converted to Christianity, 
she still made that condition to reflect the wish of her people. Emperor Valens 
accepted her situation because of his strong desire to make peace with those 
united tribes.  
Moses Refused to be Ordained by Arian Hands: 
On arriving at Alexandria, Moses found there Lucius the Arian archbishop 
who took over St. Mark's throne by force from the 20 th Pope St. Athanasius 
the Apostolic (328-373). All the other Orthodox bishops were in exile. Then , 
St. Moses stood amid St. Mark Cathedral and said with a loud voice: “Even 
though I am not worthy of the honor of a bishop, yet I consented in response 
to the love of those who chose me and gave me their trust. Yet, I shall never 
accept to be ordained by the hand of one of the deniers of the Divinity of my 
beloved Lord and Savior. If you let me be ordained by an Orthodox bishop, I 
shall accept from his hand this great honor. However, if you do not agree, 
then let me go back to my seclusion in the desert.” 
The Emperor's men tried in vain to make Moses change his mind, and they 
failed in trying to convince queen Mavia to stop her support for the monk 
Moses or to make her people choose somebody else. Finally, they had to take 
the monk to the nearest location o f the exiled Orthodox bishops, where he 
was ordained amid the exultation of the people. The people's joy was mixed 
with admiration of monk Moses, who bravely refused to submit to his tyrant 
opponents and exposed the falseness and helplessness of the Arians.  
Bishop Moses went to the flock that loved him and respected him, 
dedicated his life and effort to serve those who supported him against the 
opponents of Orthodoxy. He kept on moving from one place to another, not 
having a steady residence, teaching, preach ing, and converting multitudes to 
Christianity, and queen Mavia finally accepted the faith. He also managed to 
establish peace between his people and the Romans. Since then, the land of 
Arabia came under the St. Mark umbrella. Finally, St. Moses reposed in  the 
year 372 AD.  
 [The Story of the Coptic Church, Bk 1, p. 347] 
 [Baring-Gould: February 7]

son in this wilderness and never depart from it, because the day you would 
leave it, all evil will come bac k to you. Stay here all your life, and I am sure

His Strife: 
St. Moses started by dwelling among the monks. Yet, because of the 
multitudes of visitors, he sought from Abba Macari us to find for him a 
secluded place, and he guided him to a separate cell, where he dwelt 
tirelessly with such tremendous spiritual strife, in an attempt to make up for 
his previous sins and evil deeds. Even though the devil kept reminding him 
of his dark past, but his spiritual guide Abba Isidore counseled him to stand 
firm in opposing the old habits which were planted deep in his soul. He 
mainly complained against the evil carnal desires of Abba Isidore, who kept 
counseling him to stand fast until the dev il would get tired of him. He gave 
him an example of a stray dog that kept standing before the shop of a butcher, 
seeking to get something from him, but when the butcher did not respond to 
it, the dog had to go somewhere else. St. Moses was painfully attacked by the 
thoughts of adultery, so viciously that he could not stay in his cell. So, he 
went to ask help from St. Isidore, who told him to go back to his cell, but he 
refused, saying to the saint: “I cannot endure any more of it. ” Father. Abba 
Isidore too k him up to the roof and asked him: “Look towards the west.” 
There, he saw an uncountable crowd of demons, in great chaos, as though 
preparing for war. He then asked him: “Look towards the east.” There, he 
saw a great number of hosts of glorious saintly an gels, about whom the saint 
said to Moses: “Look, these have been sent by God to help the saints, against 
those in the west. Those who are on our side are far more than those who are 
against us.” Afterward, Moses was encouraged, gave thanks to God, and 
returned to his cell.  
Obeying the counsel of his father of confession, Moses fatigued his body 
by standing a long time in prayers, fasting, and doing metanoias. To 
discipline his body further, he used to go around the cells of the older monks 
at night, take t heir water pots and fill them with water from a well at a far 
distance from the monastery. Getting fed up with his harsh strife, the devils 
caught him once at the well, beat him so violently, and left him unable to 
move, until some brethren happened to com e to the well, and they carried 
him to the church to Abba Isidore. He cared for him for three days until he

giving his sister Sarah in marriage and handing their whole wealth to her. 
However, when he discussed the idea with his sister, she responded to him by 
saying: “If you get married first, then I would follow suit.” He told her: “I 
have committed so many sins, which I intend to atone for by leading a 
monastic life, for I cannot get married and care for my salvation at the  same 
time.” She answered him: “How would you cast me in the snares of this 
world, and care only for your salvation?” Then, he answered her: “Whatever 
you choose will be yours.” She responded: “All that you would do, I shall 
also do, for we are of one fath er and one mother.” Then, they distributed all 
their wealth to the poor and the needy. St. Moises brought his sister Sarah 
into a house of virgins, and he joined a monastery near Alexandria, and for 
the following ten years, they did not see one another.  
Their Martyrdom: 
Then, when Emperor Decius (249-251 AD) incited persecution against the 
Christians, in the days of the 14 th Pope St. Dionysius the Great (246 -264 
AD), so many believers were martyred. At that time, St. Moises sent to his 
sister to bid her fa rewell, and let her know of his decision to be martyred in 
the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. She hastened to her mother -superior, 
sought to be released, got the blessings of her sisters, and joined her brother 
on his way to Alexandria. There, they both co nfessed together the Lord Jesus 
Christ, and after being tortured by many tools, they had their heads cut off by 
the sword, and they received the crowns of martyrdom.  
 [The Synaxarion: 26 Mesra] 
 
MOISES, BISHOP OF OSIM, ST. 
St. Moises (Moses) was one of th e prominent fathers and saints of the 
church in the 8 th century AD. He was raised on the love of virginity and 
purity since his childhood, and he studied the church's various subjects.  
St. Moises became a monk, since his youth in the wilderness of the Sce tis, 
where he lived in the obedience of a great hermit for eighteen years, during 
which he walked along the road of virtue and harsh asceticism. He became 
known for his virtues that he was chosen to be the bishop of Osim (Ouseem), 
in the district of Embaba in the Beĥeira governorate. His life as a bishop was 
an extension of his monastic one in the wilderness. He was living in a life of 
deprivation and was known for his piety, courage, and zeal on the Orthodox 
faith. He used to spend most of his time in wors hip, that it was said that he 
did not see anyone, except on Saturdays and Sundays.

MOSES THE HERMIT 
St. Moses, the hermit, was born in Alexandria. Once he reached the age of 
thirteen years, he set forth to the wilderness of the Scetis. There, he dwelt for 
twenty years in a small cell next to one of the older monks. Then, he went 
deep in the wilderness an d lived for thirty -five years in a spot having olive 
and palm trees. There, he ate according to his needs whatever would fall from 
the trees, drank from the rainwater, dressed in palm leaves, and befriended 
the wild beasts.  
His Multiple Falls and Repentances:  
Satan envied this hermit, so he appeared to him in the form of an older 
man. The older man told him that he used to live a corrupt life, but he 
repented and distributed his wealth to the poor. He lived in one of the Five 
Western Cities (Pentapolis) near Cyrenaica (Barqa), and that God revealed to 
him that the hour of his death was approaching. They walked together in the 
wilderness until they reached a grand mansion. Then, the older man told the 
hermit that after his death, that mansion would be his, if he would marry his 
daughter. Moses was deceived and thought that the older man was on the 
brink of extinction, so he accepted his offer. However, once he declared his 
acceptance, he found himself amid the wilderness, hungry and afraid. He 
could not see any mansion there, and he realized that it was a trick from the 
devil. He felt how he was so weak and offered sincere repentance.  
Once St. Moses also went to Alexandria, where the devil appeared to him

MOSES, THE CONFESSOR 
This St. Moses (Moyses) was a Roman priest of Jewish roots. He was one 
of the main members of a congregation of confessors in the time of Cyprian, 
at the start of the heresy of Novat ian.1 The rest of the confessors were: Fr. 
Maximus, the priest, the two deacons Nicostratus and Rufinus, the laymen 
Urbanus, Sidonius, Macarius, and Celerinus. According to Cyprian, they 
were the first group of confessors in the days of the persecution st irred up by 
Emperor Decius (249 -251 AD). At the time of the persecution, they wrote 
down a message to exhort the confessors in Carthage to be committed to the 
system and wrote another message to Cyprian.  
After spending about a year in prison (eleven month s and few days), St. 
Moses reposed in January 251 AD, and was counted as a confessor, and even 
as a martyr. It was said that a little while before his departure, Moses refused 
to have any contact with Novatian or the five priests who were supporting 
him and followed his views. St. Moses was considering their faith and views 
as unorthodox.  
 [A Dictionary of Christian Biography, Vol. III, p. 948] 
 [Baring-Gould: November 25] 
 
MOSES, THE RECLUSE BISHOP , ST. 
The Tribes of Saracens: 
The Arabian tribes populatin g the area of Rhinoclura in -between the 
eastern Egyptian border and the Asian shores, used to worship the stars. Then 
in the year 226 AD, these tribes embraced Christianity through the efforts of 
Origen (184-253 AD). Then, those tribes 2 joined forces toge ther and formed 
one State under the reign of a queen called Mavia. By their unity, they 
created a power block that brought fear to the Arian Emperor Valens (364 -
378 AD) and forced him to seek a peace treaty with them.  
Choosing Moses as a Bishop: 
Those Chr istian tribes having united together, they felt the need for a 
bishop to shepherd them. It happened that in those days, there was a recluse 
monk named Moses in the eastern desert, he was so beloved by those 
tribesmen that they decided to choose him to be t heir bishop. Then, when

was given by the Greeks and the Romans to the nomadic tribes in the ‘Sino-Arabian’ desert…

records.question: Who was St. Mary the Egyptian?
records.answer:
St. Mary the Egyptian was a significant figure in the Coptic Orthodox Church, known for her profound repentance and ascetic life. She lived during the 4th and 5th centuries AD and is often celebrated for her transformation from a life of sin to one of holiness. Her story is primarily recounted by a priest named Zosimus, who encountered her in the desert.

Initially, Mary led a life of indulgence and sin, engaging in a lifestyle that was far removed from the teachings of Christ. However, upon realizing the emptiness of her life, she sought redemption. A pivotal moment came when she attempted to enter the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem but was mysteriously prevented from doing so. This experience led her to a deep sense of remorse and a desire to change her ways. She then prayed for forgiveness and vowed to live a life of penance.

After her conversion, Mary retreated to the desert, where she lived in solitude for many years, dedicating herself to prayer and fasting. She became known for her extreme asceticism, living off very little and spending her days in deep contemplation. Her life of repentance was marked by a profound humility and a desire to seek God above all else. Zosimus, who later found her, described her as having crossed a river on foot, a miraculous event that demonstrated her sanctity and connection to God [2].

Mary's life serves as a powerful example of the possibility of redemption and the transformative power of God's grace. She is celebrated in the Coptic Church, with her feast day observed on the 16th of Baramouda, and her story continues to inspire many in their spiritual journeys [2].

Bethany, the sister of Martha (Luke 10:38 -42) and Mary Magdalene. 
According to the Eastern Tradition, they were considered to be three different 
persons, whereas according to the Western Tradition 1, the three of them are 
considered to be one person (the sinful woman, Mary, the sister of Martha, 
and Mary Magdalene). However, St. Ambrose (374 -397 AD) was on the 
opinion th at this issue should be left unanswered. In any case, the Western 
Tradition views St. Mary Magdalene as a fantastic role model for the 
repentant person. Since 1969, the Eastern tradition has been taken into 
consideration in the New Western Roman calendar. St. Mary Magdalene is 
celebrated by the Western Church on the 22nd of July.  
 [The Penguin Dictionary of Saints, p. 230] 
 
MARY, THE ARMENIAN (The martyr) 
A Brave Captive gets martyred: 
This St. Mary was a captive of a Muslim man, one of the soldiers of the  
Mamluk Sultan of Egypt Al-Zahir Rukn al-Din Baibars (1260-1277 AD). Her 
master tried to persuade her to deny her faith in the Lord Christ. But, she 
refused to go along and proclaimed that she was a true Christian. The man 
viciously tortured her in his hou se while she held fast to her faith. When the 
man got tired of tormenting her without any results, he finally reported her to 
the Sultan using falsehood, saying, “I have a Muslim maidservant who claims 
to be a Christian.” The Sultan brought her before him and asked her to 
declare her Islam, which she refrained to do and persisted on confessing her 
Christian faith. The Sultan ordered his men to burn her alive. They dug a 
large pit at the gate of Zoweila in Cairo, where a great multitude came to 
watch. Then, they brought Mary to the edge of the fiery pit to scare her up 
and force her to change her mind. However, the saint bravely shouted : “It is 
great for me, O Sultan, to deliver my soul into the hands of my Lord God and 
Savior Jesus Christ.” Then, she quickly jumped into fire, where she received 
the crown of martyrdom. 
 [The Synaxarion: 27 Mesra] 
 
MARY, THE EGYPTIAN, ST. 
St. Mary, the Egyptian lived in the 4 th and 5 th centuries AD, and her 
biography was told by a priest called Zosimus, who lived in one of the

and then she crossed the river walking on the water. Seeing that miracle, the 
priest Zosimus attempted to bow before her. She cried out loudly, “O Father 
priest, what are you doing? Did you forget that you are carrying the Holy 
Sacraments?” She then approached, worshipped with reverence, took the 
Holy Sacraments, then raised her hands toward heaven, crying out: “Lord, let 
your servant depart in peace, for my eyes have seen Your Salvation .” (Luke 
2:29-30) She asked him to come to her in the following year, in the same 
place, to pray for her. She made the sign of the Cross on the river, crossed it 
back walking on the water, and disappeared from his sight. 
Her Departure: 
In the following year, and in the appointed time, the priest se t forth to the 
designated place, where he found the saint worshipping to the ground, with 
her face directed toward the East, and her hands motionless. Perceiving that 
she was already dead, he worshipped beside her, cried, and prayed on her the 
funeral prayers. Up to this moment, he realized that he did not even come to 
know her name; but when he got close to her, he found a written message 
saying, “Father Zosimus! Bury here the body of the miserable Mary and 
leave to the dust this sinful body. Pray on my behalf.”  
Fr. Zosimus realized that she died the year before after she had the Holy 
Sacraments he brought for her. It is believed that she reposed in the year 421 
AD. Returning to his monastery, Fr. Zosimus kept saying to himself: “Indeed, 
the tax -collectors, the sinners and the adulterers will precede us to the 
Kingdom of Heaven.” St. ‘Mary’s life was a big motivator for so many to 
expand their spiritual strive. The Coptic Church celebrates her feast on the 
16th of Baramouda every year. 
[Fragrant Bouquets from the Biographies of the Righteous and Saints, pp. 249-253] 
[The Vita of St. Mary of Egypt written by St. Sophronius, the patriarch of 
Jerusalem (634–638 AD)] 
 
MARY, THE ISRAELITE (The martyr) 
During the early life of St. Mary, the Israelite, she did not know the Lord 
Christ, and she led a sinful life. When she wanted to repent and to return to 
the righteous life, the Lord sent to her a saintly man who preached her and 
revealed to her the way of  salvation through believing in the Lord Christ. He 
told her that the soul would have to give an answer for all her deeds on the 
Day of Resurrection. After death and departure from this world, everyone 
will be rewarded according to his deeds. The man explained to her the fearful 
punishments for the evildoers. She asked him: "What are the proofs to what 
you have said to me since the ‘Torah’ that God gave to ‘Moses the Prophet’
