6- Another time, he came down to Alexandria to support the confessors in 
prison and accompany them to the arena of martyrdom. 
7- With his great love of seclusion, he took St. Macarius the Great, who 
founded the system of congregations; as one of his disc iples and greatly 
rejoiced to hear the news of St. Pachomius, the founder of the order of 
fellowship and commended him for it. He carried no prejudice to any 
particular order. 
8- His seclusion did not have a feeling of boredom; for all were amazed to 
see his outer cheerfulness and inner exultation. He enjoyed good health 
until the day he reposed, having reached 105 years of age. 
9- Even though he was illiterate and did not know how to read or write, yet 
he could overcome the Greek philosophers by his pure heart, and also 
drew some of them to faith. Moreover, when he was asked how he could 
find comfort in the middle of the mountains without having a book, he 
answered that God comforted him through the mind, which preceded the 
written text. 
When he was asked about the meaning of a verse that came in the Book 
of the Hebrews, he raised his eyes toward the wilderness, and then cried out 
seeking from God to send the prophet Moses to interpret its meaning to him. 
Instantly, a voice was heard talking to him; and according to Abba 
Ammonius, they also heard the voice, though did not comprehend it. 
Of His Words: 
 Our life and death are with our neighbor. If we gain our neighbor, we have 
gained God; and if we offend him, we sinned against Christ. 
 Some have burdened their bodies with asceticism; but because of the lack 
of discernment, they stayed away from God. 
 There will come a time when men are so inflicted with craziness, that if 
they see someone prudent, they attack him, saying: You are crazy; you are 
not like us. 
 Obedience and forsaking worldly pleasures grant men the authority over 
the beasts of the wilderness. 
The Church celebrates his departure on the 22nd of Toba. 
 [The Biography of Abba Anthony by Abba Athanasius the Apostolic -- Translated 
by Hegumen Marcos Daoud] 
 
ANTIOCHUS AND CYRIAC 
(The martyrs) 
These saints were martyred in the 3 rd century AD in ‘Sebaste’ during the

161 
 
at the ninth hour and would reach it before sunset. Shortly after, those pious 
monks started to build cells there, and the region was called ‘the cells’ zone. 
His Personality and the Role of Nitria; 
Abba Amon did not achieve such exalted fame like that of St. Anthony or 
St. Macarius, who started after him, because of his personality. He was 
characterized with great humility and shyness and had a tendency to fly away 
from the crowd and refrained from performing a ny miracles, claiming that he 
was not given that gift. However, that does not lessen in any way the high value 
of his vital role in developing the monastic movement. He was its founder in 
that region, and so many of his disciples became great fathers. The closeness 
of ‘Nitria’ zone to the inhabited area, along with the fame of its fathers, caused 
so many problems for the church. The Arians and the Chalcedonians attempted 
to impose their authority on the church through the submission of those fathers. 
Hence, after those two zones (Nitria & the Cells) have flourished, a counter 
migration movement of monks started from it right after the repose of Abba 
Amon. 
St. Palladius visited the region of Nitria, about a half a century after the 
repose of Abba Amon, where he estimated the number of the monks to be 5000, 
among whom there were 600 recluses; all practicing handiwork. And, he also 
found there a considerable church and next to it a house of retreat for the 
guests, with eight priests to minister in the church.  
His Miracles: 
Some farmers once came to Abba Amon, carrying a little child mauled by a 
dog and suffering severe pain. The saint asked them: “Why should you come 
to me to do something beyond my worthiness, when, in your hands, you have 
the healing medicine f or this child?! Now, give the stolen cow back to its 
widow owner, and the child will be healed." Having perceived that the saint 
revealed their hidden sin, they presented repentance and gave the cow back to 
its owner. The saint then prayed for the child, and the Lord healed him. 
St. Athanasius told that story about St. Amon: He was once with his disciple 
‘Tadros,’ and they needed to cross a river. Known for his great shyness, he 
sought from his disciple to go away from him, for each of them to take his 
clothes off and swim. Despite doing that, Abba Amon was too shy to take his 
clothes off, even in the absence of his disciple. In the middle of his confusion, 
he found himself all of a sudden on the other shore of the river. When his 
disciple saw him there with  his dry clothes, he was persistence to know how 
he crossed over. The saint told him, seeking from him not to tell it to anyone 
before his repose. 
His repose:

two brothers; Paul decided to take the matter to court . However, on his way 
to court, he encountered a very wealthy man's funeral procession, happened 
to be passing by . St. Paul asked himself: “Has t hat rich man taken anything 
from this world with him?” Then, he had a complete change of heart and he 
totally despised the temporal life . His heart was so i nflamed with the Eternal 
inheritance, that instead of going to the court, he got out of the city and  
entered into a deserted tomb where he spent three days praying and seeking 
the Divine guidance. 
Then, an angel appeared to St . Paul and guided him to the wilderness in 
the East Desert, where he dwelt in mount Nimra, near the Red Sea . There he 
lived for eighty years. During all these years he saw no one, clothed himself 
in a tunic made of palm tree leaves and God sustained him with a daily ration 
of half a loaf of bread, which was carried to him by a raven . The saint lived 
all that time on that bread with s ome dates from the palm trees or herbs from 
the mountain, and he drank water from a nearby spring. 
An Encounter with Abba Anthony: 
One time, St. Anthony the Great was thinking that he was the first man to 
dwell in that wilderness . Then, an  angel of the Lor d appeared to Abba  
Anthony and told him about the presence of a very special man, whom the 
world was unworthy of his footsteps; and for the sake of his prayers , God has 
lifted the drought from the world and has granted it plenty of rain. 
On hearing that Heavenly testimony, St . Anthony set forth  with Divine 
guidance, to the cave of St . Paul. When he got there, St . Paul called him by 
his name and they sat together talking about the great works of God in their 
lives. At sunset, the raven came as usual  but carrying a whole loaf of bread . 
St. Paul then said: “Now I know for sure that you are a man of God; for all 
along eighty years the raven kept providing me with only half a loaf of bread, 
but today it came with a whole loaf. God sent you your food.” 
At the end of their talk, Abba Paul sought from Abba Anthony to hasten to 
bring him the priestly garment of the 20th Pope of Alexandria, St. Athanasius 
the Apostolic (328-373 AD); for his departure time was approaching . Abba 
Anthony returned greatly affected, brought the garment , and headed back to 
St. Paul's cave. On his way, he saw a group of angels carrying his s oul to 
Paradise, while joyfully singing praise to God. 
On reaching the cave of Abba Paul, Abba Anthony found him kneeling . 
For a moment, he assumed that he was praying, so he waited for him to 
finish. Finally, he realized that he has reposed in the Lord and he intensely 
mourned him. This happened on the 2nd of Amshir in the year 343 AD.  
When St. Antony wanted to bury St . Paul, he wondered how he could dig 
the grave, then two lions entered the cave, bowed their heads before the body

This saint was born in the year 294 AD near Marriott; and like his colleague 
‘Anthony,' he was of a wealthy pious family. He lost his parents while still in 
his youth and became under the guardianship  of his uncle. He desired to live 
as a virgin; his uncle betrothed for him a rich girl against his will. Not able to 
disobey his uncle ’s wish, he kept talking to his betrothed girl with spiritual 
conviction and through his holy behavior, he managed to have a good impact 
on her and made her love purity and planted in her heart the desire to dedicate 
her soul to be a bride for the real Groom Jesus Christ. The couple agreed to go 
along with the wedding plan, yet persisted on living together like brother and 
sister. They remained for 17 years, strict ly keeping their virginity. After that 
period, the wife departed to the eternal kingdom. In a night vision, the saint 
saw Abba Anthony calling him to put on the monastic ‘Eskeem.' Waking up, 
he went to St. Isidore who put on him the holy Eskeem. He stayed with him 
for some time; then, he set forth to Mount Tuna, where St. Anthony was 
dwelling. He lived a period with St. Anthony and became his disciple. He 
learned from him the holy monastic rules, then the saint built for him a cave in 
Mount Tuna and strove there in so many ways.  
The devil envied him and came to him in the form of a nun knocking at his 
door. When he opened the door and sought her to pray, the devil turned into a 
flame of fire and went away. Then, the devil seduced a loose woman to try to 
make the saint fall in sin. So, she put on her best attire and came at sunset and 
knocked on the saint’s door, saying: “I am a stranger traveler, who lost my way. 
It is now close to night time. Do not leave me outside, lest a beast may devour 
me, and you shall be responsible for my blood." The saint opened the door for 
her and recognized the trick of the devil who sent her, so he began to preach 
her from the Bible, to warn her about the suffering in hell prepared for the 
sinners and told her about the happines s prepared for the righteous. God 
opened up her heart; she understood his sayings and threw herself at his feet, 
weeping and supplicating to him to help her save her soul. He made her discard 
her luxurious clothes, had her head shaved, clothed her in a woo len garment 
and called her ‘The Naïve.' He taught her the way of virtues, and she followed 
it very well. She surpassed some saints by her fasting and persistent prayers. 
When the devil kept failing in his attempts to trip up the saint, he tried

THEOGNOSTUS, FR. 
He was a priest from Alexandria, who was sent as a deputy of the 24th Pope 
Cyril the Great (412-444 AD) to Constantinople, along with Fr. Sharmocinus 
the priest and Liontius the deacon [Cyril: Letters 37, 41] 
      [Smith & Wace; Vol 4, p. 990] 
 
THEOGNOSTUS 
Theognostus (Theogust) was a priest and a theologian in Alexandria in the 
3rd century AD. He was the Dean of the School of Alexandria, most probably 
before Fr. Peros. About him, we know very little through quotations that came 
in the writings of Fotius, Athanasius, and Gregory bishop of Nyssa. 
His doctrinal work “Hypotyposes” came in seven books, these books were 
available in the time of Fotius, but they have been lost later on . In his first 
book, he followed the style of Origen . In the second and third books, there 
were some Arian tendencies. In the fifth book, he denoted bodies to the angels 
and demons.While in the sixth and seventh books, he dealt with the Divine 
Incarnation in a sound Orthodox manner . The 20 th Pope Athanasius  the 
Apostolic considered his work as one of the best testimonies against Arianism. 
 
THEON, THE BLESSED ABBA 
This saint met with St. Jerome (347 -420) when he visited the region of 
Thebes. He was a monk who lived 30 years far from the city of Oxyrhync hus 
(El-Bahnasa)1 on the border of the extensive wilderness . He stayed in a little 
house he built by himself, keeping silent and practicing worship with such an 
enflamed heart, to be considered by the people as a prophet . And, with the 
spread of the sweet fragrance of Christ through his life, vast multitudes of 
people came daily to him carrying their sick . He used to stretch his hand on 
them from the window, and they were healed in the name of the Lord. 
It happened that some thieves, assuming that the hermit must have acquired 
plenty of gold from the gifts of his visiting people, so they came to kill him by 
night. Finding him standing in prayers, they were cast around as though 
chained by ropes and remained as such until the morning. When the multitudes 
came, as usual, they planned to punish them, but the saint sought from them to 
leave them alone, lest the Lord would take the gift of healing away from him . 
When they did, the thieves came to him with remorse and the fear of God and 
joined the rank of monks to practice the life of fellowship with God. 
 
1 ‘Oxyrhynchus’ (El-Bahnasa) is about 160 km south-southwest of Cairo in ‘El-Minya’ governorate…

297 
 
IBRAHIM, THE ANCHORITE, ST. 
Ibrahim was a Pachomian monk whose feast is celebrated by the Church on 
the 30th of Baba. He was born in the city of Menuf to a wealthy pious family. 
He grew up despising every pleasure of this world. When he came to the proper 
age, he set out to Akhmim in Upper Egypt, and then from there , he went to 
where St. Pachomius resided. He revealed to him the longings of his heart . 
After being tested by St. Pachomius, he put on him the monastic attire.  
This saint practiced the life of communion and fellowship with loyalty and 
outstanding love toward his brothers’ monks for twenty-three years. Yet, when 
he started longing for a life of seclusion, he was allowed by St. Pachomius to 
live in a separate cave outside of the monastery. There, he led a strict monastic 
life, occupying himself with making fishing nets . Somebody from the 
community helped him by selling his hand -work, and buying him beans and 
giving the rest of the money to the poor. His daily food was a few beans wetted 
in water. His clothes, which he never replaced, were so worn out  that he used 
a piece of sackcloth to cover himself. He encountered no one and never came 
out of his cell, except to have the Holy Communion once every two or th ree 
years. 
Feeling that his time to depart from this world had come, he sent for his 
dear friend St. Tadros , the disciple of St. Pachomius . St. Tadros came and 
prayed with him for a while ; then, St. Ibrahim made the sign of the Cross on 
himself, and his soul departed into the Lord. 
       [The Synaxarion 30 Baba] 
 
IGNATIUS, THE THEOPHORUS, ST. 
He was born around the year 30 A.D. and was raised in Syria. Some scholars 
believe that he was the child whom the Lord Jesus Christ carried when He 
presented him as an example of humility (Matt. 18:2-4). 
Seeing his kindled zeal, the apostles ordained him a s a bishop on Antioch. 
However, there was a disagreement concerning which apostle has ordained 
him. According to some, Peter, the apostle, ordained Evodius as a bishop for 
the Christians from Jewish origin; and John, the apostle, ordained Ignatius for 
the Christians from Gentile origin . When bishop Evodius reposed, bishop 
Ignatius was put in charge of the region' s Christians from both origins. Being 
known for his eagerness for the salvation of souls, he gained so many new 
Gentiles for the Lord Christ. His i ntense love for his people was recorded in 
his conversation with those who came to welcome him in Smyrna, during his 
trip to Rome to be martyred. He kept mentioning his congregation to them and 
asked them to pray for his people.

these thoughts and had understood the meaning of the rock, which is Christ. For she says: 
‘Show me your face, and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and  your 
countenance is glorious’ … And those who hear his sweet voice know the grace of the 
gospel—the ones who say, ‘You have the words of eternal life’ (John 6:68).”1091  
538. Why does St. Ignatius, the Theophorus, call the Church “a congregation of love”? 
St. Ignatius the Theophorus says, “All these things are good together, if you believe in 
love.”1092 He also says that Christ is eternal life for He grants us life through His divine love, 
“for the drink of God is His blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.”1093  
539. Why does St. Ignatius the Theophorus call the Church “a congregation of 
thanksgiving and praise”? 
Because in the Eucharist, the Church is manifested in two ways. The first way is through 
love, purity, unity, fellowship in immortality, along wit h joy and praise. The second way is 
by resisting the devil and conquering him. St. Ignatius the Theophorus says, “Take heed, 
then, often to come together to give thanks to God, and show forth His praise. For when you 
assemble frequently in the same place, the powers of Satan are destroyed, and the destruction 
at which he aims is prevented by the unity of your faith.”1094  
540. How does Christ work in the members of His Church? 
Origen says, “When the Churches of God which are instructed by Christ, are carefully 
contrasted with the assemblies of the districts in which they are situated, they are as beacons 
in the world.”1095  
541. What is the Church’s role in the hearts of believers? 
According to a Syrian author, the role played by the Church, here on earth, is to inflame 
our hearts with longing to the heavenly Church: “It is befitting for us not to despise the seen 
church, which begets every one of us as children. Let us also not despise the church of the 
heart, which strengthens those who are sick. We must long to the high er (heavenly) church 
which perfects all the saints.”1096  
 
1091 St. Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory of Nyssa: Homilies on The Song of Songs, ed., Brian E. Daley S.J. and 
John T. Fitzgerald, trans., Richard A. Norris Jr. (Society of Biblical Literature, 2012) 5: pp. 175–177.

which he declined. After promising to give him many honors if he denied his 
Christ, he rejected them and held fast to his faith . Then, they started torturing 
him. They whipped him, pressed him by the Henbazin, cut some of his limbs, 
and burned his sides with fire . In all this, he endured for his love of the Lord 
Christ. And, the Lord sent his angel to strengthen and comfort him . Finally, 
they cut his head off, and he received the crown of martyrdom.  
The Church celebrated his feast on the 28th of Amshir. 
 
THEODORE, SON OF JULIUS EL-AQFAHSY (The martyr) 
This St. Theodore  was the son of the great martyr Julius el-Aqfahsy, the 
writer of the biographies of the martyrs . Together with his father, his brother 
Unias, their servants, the governors of Samannoud and Atrib, with a  great 
multitude of 1,500 believers were martyred all together. His body and those of 
his father and brother were moved to Alexandria on the 22nd of Tout. 
 
THEODORET, THE NESTORIAN HISTORIAN 
This Theodoret was a bishop of Cyrus (Cyrrhus)1, a citizen of Antioch, and 
educated in Antioch Monastic School. He distributed his possession on the 
poor and joined the Nicerte monastery around the year 416 A D when he was 
about 23 years of age. He was ordained as a bishop in Syria in the year 423 AD 
against his own will , and he was a strong adversary against paganism , In the 
controversy between the 24th pope of Alexandria St. Cyril the Great (412-444) 
and the heretic Nestor (428-431 AD), he took the side of his friend Nestor. But 
contrary to his friend Nestor, who refused to call the Virgin Mary, by the title 
Theotokos, namely (the Mother of God), Theodoret accepted it as a symbolic 
meaning. In the Council of Ephesus (431 AD), he strongly opposed pope Cyril 
the Great and the decrees of the Holy Council; although St. Cyril himself has 
accepted earlier a decree of faith, craftily written by Theodoret in the year 430.  
In the year 448 AD, he was accused by the 25 th pope of Alexandria St. 
Dioscorus I (444-454) that he made the Lord Christ as two Persons, for which 
he was considered as a heretic and was exiled from his throne. He was released 
from exile after appealing to Emperor Marcian (450-457). He then took part in 
the Chalcedonian Council in 451 AD against St. Dioscorus I. 
The Western Church tried to defen d him by claiming that he forsook the 
Nestorian heresy after the year 451 AD... 
This Theodoret left several works, among which were the interpretations of 
the Books of the Old and the New Testaments. Some of those were in the form

Eusebius makes frequent use of Dionysius’
letters as an important source of the history of his life and times. He sent a
letter to Novatius who was illegally ordained the Bishop of Rome. In his
letter, he tactfully asked him to retire from the post even if he would be
martyred, for avoiding schism is more glorious than martyrdom.
“For in the
one case a man is a martyr for the sake of his own single soul, but in the
other for the sake of the whole Church."
[314]
Another letter he addressed to Basilides,
Bishop of Pantopolis in which he answers several questions regarding the
duration of Lent and the physical conditions required for the reception of the
Eucharist.
The third letter is addressed to Fabius,
Bishop of Antioch, in which he deals with the vexing problem of forgiveness
after apostasy during persecution. In his letter, he recounts the following:
I shall set forth for you this one example that happened amongst us:
There was a certain Serapion amongst us, an old man and a believer, who lived
blamelessly for a long time, but in time of the trial fell. This man oftentimes
besought (absolution), and no one paid him heed. For indeed he had sacrificed.
And, falling sick, he continued for three successive days speechless and
unconscious; but on the fourth day he rallied a little, and calling his
grandson to him, he said: “How long, my child, do you hold me back? Haste you,
I pray, and grant me one of the presbyters.” And having said this he again
became speechless. The boy ran for the presbyter. But it was night, and he was
unwell and could not come. Yet since I had given an order that those who were
departing this life, if they besought it, and especially if they had made
supplication before, should be absolved, that they might depart in hope, he
gave the little boy a small portion of the Eucharist, bidding him soak it and
let it fall in drops down into the old man’s mouth.
The fourth letter (
On Martyrdom
) is
addressed to the great master Origen

who was in prison at Tyre.
Finally, Eusebius mentions the Paschal
letters written every year by Dionysius in which he announces the date of
Easter and the beginning of the Lent. These letters took the form of pastoral

Because of
widespread persecution, historical sources differ in arranging the Deans of the

contradictory, yet they were actually complementing each other. They were: 
+ Refraining from eating bread would calm down the body of the monk. 
+ The continuous hunger would make the monk frail, and might even lead

 [W. Budge: The Paradise; Vol. 2, p. 21: 253] 
 
THEODOTUS, BISHOP OF ANCYRA 
Bishop Theodotus was a supporter of the Nestorian theology of the heretic 
Nestor. However, in the Council of Ephesus in the year 431 AD, he reversed 
his position and becam e a prominent supporter of the 24th Pope St. Cyril of 
Alexandria (412-444) against Nestor.  This bishop  was defrocked by the 
Nestorians at their Synod of Tarsus in th e year 432 A D. Bishop Theodotus 
wrote so many articles, among which were: Essays against Ne stor (lost); an 
explanation of the Nicene Creed of Faith; several essays on the feast of 
Nativity; and on the Purification . Also, there is a mymar which has been 
attributed to him, dealing with the martyrdom of St. George and his miracles... 
 
THEODULUS AND AGATHOPUS (The martyrs) 
At the beginning of the 4th century AD, St. Agathopus the deacon and St. 
Theodulus the lector (reader), were martyred in the city of Thessalonica during 
the reign of Emperor Maximianus  (286-305). Faustinus, governor of the city, 
put them under arrest and sought from them to deny their Christ. On refusing 
to do so, he cast them in jail. There, the Lord wanted to put them at ease, so He 
allowed them to see a vision: They were as though sailing in a ship, which did 
encounter a violent storm that broke the ship and brought it down. Swimming 
along, they both reached a rock and ascended a hill peacefully. The two saints 
perceived that they would be encountering a great tribulation that would end 
up in their meeting with the Lo rd Christ – the True Rock – and to ascend to 
His Heavenly Paradise. Indeed, by refusing to deliver the books of the Church 
to the governor, after torturing them, he ordered to tie massive rocks to their 
necks and to cast them into the sea . There, their bodies were discovered later 
on in a miraculous way. They were martyred on the 4th of April 303 AD.

In Troas: 
He was taken in a boat from Smyrna to Troas, where he wrote three more 
letters to Philadelphia, Smyrna, and St. Polycarp. From Troas , he sailed to 
Neopolis, to Philippi, then to Epirus and Tyrone. Finally, he arrived at the 
region of Portus, where he met with the brethren, whose joy to see him was 
mixed with the sadness of his close departure. He received them with love, 
asking them to have the courage and show him true love. 
He knelt and prayed to God to put an end to the wave of persecution against 
His Church and to increase the love of the brethren toward each other. 
Finally, the guards rushed him to the arena and released the wild beasts, 
which he received with a cheerful countenance. Two lions jumped on him and 
devoured him to leave off his body, only a few bones. The believers gathered 
his precious relics and sent them to Antioch. His martyrdom took place around 
the year 108 AD. The Church celebrates him on the 7th of Abib. 
[Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty: The Two Martyrs: Ignatius and Polycarp; 1964] 
 
INNOCENT, BISHOP OF TORTONA, ST. 
This saint was born in Tortona in the north of Italy . His heart  was so 
inflamed with the love of God, that he was called before the judges charged of 
being a Christian. On refusing to deny his faith, he fell under torture and was 
finally included in a list of the condemned to be burned alive. However, before 
his execution, he saw in a dream his father asking him to go at once to Rome 
to find safety. When he woke up, he found the guards sleeping deeply, and he 
managed to flee quickly. 
In Rome, St. Innocent was received kindly by Pope Militiades (311-314 
AD) bishop of Rome . Then, his successor Pope Sylvester I (314 -335 AD) 
ordained him as a deacon. After the accession of the Emperor Constantine the 
Great (306-337 AD), the pope sent back  St. Innocent to Tortona as a bishop . 
During the twenty-eight years of his pastoral service as a bishop, St. Innocent 
cared to spread the faith among pagans and to convert the pagan temples , 
which became vacant of worshippers, into churches , as well as to build new 
churches. He departed around the year 350 AD. 
 [Butler's Lives of Saints, p.112 - April 17]

This Roman pope was born in Albano near Rome, and succeeded St. 
Anastasius (399-401 AD) on the Seat of Rome around the year 401 . During

This St. Theophilus  was one of the Christian apologists . However, only 
three books survived out of his many written works . Those books were 
dedicated to his pagan friend Autolycus, in which he introduced the Christi an 
thoughts about God and His creation before the pagan world with its wrong 
diverse fantasies. Among his lost writings were essays against Marcion and the 
heresy of Hermogenes. 
Of his Sayings: 
+ No one can see God except those who are capable of seeing Him, when their 
souls’ eyes are open wide . When there is dirt on a mirror, man cannot see 
his face in it. Likewise, it is with the sinful. He cannot see God. 
+ I indeed honor the emperor, yet not by worshipping him, but by praying for 
him. 
 
THEOPHILUS, The 23rd POPE OF ALEXANDRIA 
The word Theophilus is of a Greek origin, meaning (the Lover of God) . It 
is being driven from two words: ‘Theo’ (=God) and ‘Philo’ (=Lover) . 
According to St. Athanasius the Apostolic; Abba Anthony the Great , in his 
youth was called Theophilus, because of his righteousness in the Lord and for 
his continuous conquests in his spiritual strife. Pope Theophilus (385-412 AD) 
was the third successor of the 20th Pope Athanasius the Apostolic (328-373), 
and he was the predecessor of his nephew the 24th Pope Cyril the Great (412-
444 AD). He sat on the papal throne for 28 years of continuous activity that 
had a great impact on the history of the Church and the State, as well. 
His life was associated with three important events: 
1- He was u prooting the paganism in Egypt , something for which many 
historians commended him.  Even though some attempted to distort his 
image by showing him as a violent tyrant, in turning the pagan temples into 
churches. Yet, as testified by history, he did  so after those temples were 
already deserted.  
2- The struggle against Origen, having become an opponent to whoever 
supported the teaching of Origen, or used his name. Hence, those Origen’s 
advocates attempted to distort the pope’s image. 
3- His opposition towards St. J ohn Chrysostom. When St. John Chrysostom 
embraced The Tall Brothers the prominent defenders of Origen ; the 
Empress Eudoxia, the wife of the Eastern Roman emperor Arcadiu s (395-
408) used the pope’s hatred against the Origenism  to lure him to send St.

Tadros the Bishop:  
The one thing we know about this saint is that he wrote to St. Augustine 
(354-430) requesting his advice about what to do with the priests who 
apostatized from the heresy of Donatism. That heresy caused a dis agreement 
in the Church, and assume d that the power of baptism depended upon the 
holiness of those who performed the Sacrament and that dissent also rejected 
the repentance of the sinners. 
St. Augustine asked the bishop to receive the priests who apostatized from 
this heresy with the proper compassion . Yet he should, at the same time, 
proclaim clearly to them that he did not accept their previous  opposition and 
that he despised th at heresy. However, he should not disregard the Name of 
God they carry; and should proclaim to them that he believed in their baptism, 
their priesthood, and their vows of virginity . He should accept them, but not 
their sins. St.Augustine requested from bishop Theodorus to show his letter

St. Theodosia (Thaodosia) was originally worshipper of idols. She was the

on the 7 th of Abib, in a martyrdom procession that preceded the saint’s, who

records.question: What does the Coptic Orthodox Church teach about purgatory?
records.answer:
The Coptic Orthodox Church does not hold a doctrine of purgatory as it is commonly understood in some other Christian traditions. Instead, it teaches that after death, the soul's fate is determined based on the life lived in the body. The Church emphasizes that the body and soul are united in faith during earthly life, and they receive their eternal reward or punishment together after death. This is articulated in the Catechism, which states, "How is it possible for a spirit in Hades to repent, when it has separated from the body and there is no possibility of declaring life to God and men?" [1]. 

According to the teachings, upon death, the soul is taken by angels if it is righteous, as seen in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, where "righteous angels came and bore his soul to the bosom of Abraham" [1]. Conversely, the souls of the wicked are taken by evil angels, indicating a clear distinction in the afterlife based on one's earthly choices and faith [1]. 

The Church teaches that there is no opportunity for repentance or change of state after death, reinforcing the idea that one's earthly life is crucial for determining their eternal destiny. Therefore, the concept of purgatory, which suggests a temporary state of purification after death, is not part of Coptic Orthodox belief. Instead, the focus is on the immediate judgment of the soul upon departure from the body, leading to either eternal communion with God or separation from Him [1][3]. 

In summary, the Coptic Orthodox Church emphasizes the importance of living a faithful life on earth, as this directly influences the soul's eternal fate, with no intermediary state like purgatory.

establish from them His divine house. The Church of the New Testament enjoys a new life 
through baptism, and is established in Christ, the firstborn of those who have fallen asleep. 
462. Do the so-called saints make up the Church? 
The believers who make up the Church are called by the Apostle Paul “to be saints” 
(Rom. 1:7; 1 Cor. 1:2, 24). They are saints because God calls them and thus, they are special 
among all their fellows. When they receive the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, they become 
consecrated to God. The Commemoration of Saints always includes priests who labored for 
the edification of the body of Christ and served the holy mysteries, so that the believers may 
be sanctified. It also includes sinful preachers who used God's Word to attract new members 
to the Church. Although the scribes and pharisees were corrupt, the Lord did not take away 
their honor from them but gave them authority despite t heir wickedness, because they 
themselves do not do what they teach others (Matt. 23:3). 
463. Can Church members who cannot be rectified be cut off from the Church? 
Although the Church, the body of Christ, portrays God’s love for humanity, there are 
limits that she will never exceed. A sinner is cut off from the fellowship of the Church since 
he isolates himself from the life and salvation that spring from her. Thus, the rebellious 
sinners who have trampled the Son of God underfoot, counted the blood of the coven ant by 
which they were sanctified a common thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace (Heb. 10:29), 
who preserves salvation within the Church — outside of which there is no salvation — set 
themselves apart from Christ and His community, the Church, and thus b reak every 
relationship with her. 
On the other hand, the heretics who misinterpret the teachings of Christ and His holy 
apostles (even if they quote phrases from the true Gospel), are excommunicated and 
separated from our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Thus St. Paul teaches, “But 
even if we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel to you than what we have 
preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again, if anyone 
preaches any other gospel to you than what you have received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 
1:8–9). St. John the Apostle forbids receiving anyone who comes and does not have the true 
teachings. It is necessary not to receive them in homes and not to greet them (2 John 10). In 
fact, St. Paul comma nds us, “Reject a divisive man after the first and second admonition, 
knowing that such a person is warped and sinning, being self -condemned” (Titus 3:10–11). 
Heretics, because of their inaccurate faith and their arrogance, persist in their false teachings 
and isolate themselves from the source of life; the faith in Christ, and so they grow lukewarm 
and are thus expelled. If we do not stand firm on the foundation of the Apostles, we will lose 
our foundation and will collapse. 932 And we become like those who wanted to return to the

24  
The Coptic Church and the Monastic Movement 
870. Is asceticism, as it is practiced in the Coptic Church, biblical? 
The Coptic Church is known for its ascetic inclinations, not only due to the monastic 
movement that started in it, but asceticism is also considered one of the essential 
characteristics manifested in her life as a whole and her worship. These inclinations exist not 
because asceticism is a goal in and of itself, nor on the basis that the flesh is evil in nature; 
but rather on a biblical and heavenly understanding: “For what profit is it to a man if he gains 
the whole world, and loses his own soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?” 
(Matt. 16:26). “Go your way, sell whatever you have and give to the poor … and follow Me” 
(Mark 10:21, Luke 18:22). “But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when 
I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27). 
This biblical understanding was found to be sweet by the Copts, whose hearts were 
inflamed with eternal love. 
871. What is the goal of ascetic life according to the Copts? 
While most ancient civilizations were attached to the temporal life and so they pursued 
worldly pleasures, the Egyptian mind was consumed with the world to come. Ancient 
Egyptians believed in the so -called “resurrection,” which is the belief in the resurrection of 
the dead to eternal life, if certain rituals were performed. This is why bodies were mummified 
in sealed tombs, such that no one would be able to visit the tomb or live in it except for the 
soul. The tombs were supplied with one’s daily needs (clothes, food, drink, vessels, knives, 
chairs, weapons, chariots, jewelry, toys for children … etc.). 
When the Copts accepted Christianity, their longing for the world to come grew, and their 
hearts were inflamed with longing for it, but now on a biblical basis. Instead of being 
concerned with the souls’ return to their bodies in the tombs, they desired for their souls, 
thoughts, and hearts to be lifted up to enjoy the heavenly life even when their bodies were 
still treading on the earth. In other words, their longing for the world to come drove them to 
lead an ascetic life on a biblical basis. 
872. What is the motive of asceticism for the Copts? 
Asceticism in the Coptic Church is not a goal in its own, but it is one’s practical response 
to the divine love. If our Lord offered His life for us, it is fitting for us to desire to offer our 
lives as a sacrifice of love to God. We despise worldly pleasures as a sign of our inner longing 
to enjoy the eternal joy of the new life in Christ Jesus. Believers, especially monks, have a

New Testament and so he chanted saying, “this is none other them the house of God and 
this is the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:17). 
Second: The era of the Mosaic Law and Prophets: The law explained in detail the 
sacrifices and their rituals as a symbol of Christ’s sacrifice. The prophets wro te many 
prophecies about the Savior, His birth, crucifixion, burial, resurrection, and ascension.  
Third: The era of the incarnation of the Logos until His ascension: The Lord revealed 
His divine love to us, so He fed the hungry, healed the sick, comforted the brokenhearted and 
revealed to them His providence even after His ascension when He sent them the Comforter, 
the Holy Spirit. He announced to them the Father’s love to all humanity and the Holy Spirit’s 
work to declare the divine truth and lead the Church to heaven as she struggles in the world.  
Fourth: The era between Christ’s ascension until His second coming: Here, He acts 
as a heavenly high priest. The Apostle Paul spoke about this era in his epistle to the Hebrews 
(Heb. 6:20) in which he compares between the high priests who were in need of redemption 
and the unique heavenly High Priest.  
453. Why does the Creed mention the Church after talking about the oneness of God 
and the Holy Trinity? 
The goal of the Orthodox Creed is not to mention some theoretical facts about God, the 
world, the Church, the final judgment, and the eternal life, but its main goal is to help the 
believer encounter God, enjoy His love as he struggles in the world, prepare him for the great 
day of the Lord, help him have com munion with the heavenly, and have eternal life. So, as 
we confess our faith saying, “ and in One Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church,” we are 
affirming our commitment to be in communion with the Holy God, to love one another, to 
have a relationship with our  friends in heaven as we join their praising choir and enjoy our 
sonship to God on an eternal level.  
Our knowledge of the Church drives us to look forward to our life in heaven when we 
depart and meet the heavenly Bridegroom who will welcome us in a joyfu l heavenly 
procession which the heavenly hosts look forward to saying, “thrust in your sickle and reap” 
(Rev. 14:15). We should not marvel that the heavenly hosts are earnestly looking forward to 
the day of the Lord, since they view our Church not as a social institution governed by some 
laws that are in place to ensure man’s happiness, but as the people of God who are being 
prepared to partake in the angelic life where the believer experiences God’s plan for him 
every day. Therefore, we should not be surprised if we hear about many of the saints such as 
St. John Chrysostom who felt that they were the happiest people in the world. The believer 
has his eyes fixed on his Creator and Savior and what He is preparing for him in heaven, so 
he is joyful in the midst of his hardships. The believer performs his job with all honesty and 
is faithful in his relationships with others, because he considers himself to be a child of God 
who does not know failure, despair, or greed as he is the ambassador of heaven on earth.

records.question: What does the Coptic Orthodox Church say about the Protestant principle of sola scriptura?
records.answer:
The Coptic Orthodox Church holds a distinct view regarding the principle of sola scriptura, which asserts that Scripture alone is the sole authority in matters of faith and practice. This principle is fundamentally at odds with the Church's understanding of tradition and the role it plays in the life of faith.

According to the Coptic Orthodox perspective, the Holy Bible is indeed a vital component of the Church's tradition, but it is not the only source of authority. The Church teaches that "the tradition of the true Church is the guardian of the Christian faith" and that true interpretation of Scripture is found within the Church itself, not in isolation from it [1]. This reflects the belief that the Church, through its traditions, has preserved and transmitted the teachings of Christ and the apostles, which include both oral and written forms of revelation.

The Coptic Orthodox Church emphasizes that the Bible was received and understood through the lens of tradition. For instance, it states that the Church "received the 'word of God' before it was written on paper" and that the Gospel is not separate from tradition but is its first component [6]. This indicates that the Church's understanding of Scripture is deeply intertwined with its traditions, which have been passed down through generations.

Furthermore, the Church acknowledges that while tradition testifies to the Holy Bible, it cannot judge it. Instead, tradition is accepted only if it aligns with the teachings of the Bible [2]. This relationship highlights the Church's view that both Scripture and tradition are essential for a complete understanding of the faith.

In summary, the Coptic Orthodox Church does not support the Protestant principle of sola scriptura, as it believes that both Scripture and tradition are necessary for understanding and living out the Christian faith. Tradition is seen as the "nervous system of the Church," essential for its existence and practice [7]. This perspective underscores the importance of the Church's teachings and the continuity of faith through both written and oral traditions.

73. What does St. Cyprian say about tradition? 
St. Cyprian insists that outside the Church there is no salvation, either for heretics or for 
schismatics: “He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his 
mother.”243 Therefore, the true interpretation of Scripture and orthodox doctrines are found 
only within the true Church. The tradition of the true Church is the guardian of the Christian 
faith. 
74. What does St. Gregory the bishop of Nyssa say about tradition? 
In the writings of St. Gregory of Nyssa, we find: “it is enough for proof of our statement, 
that the tradition has come down to us from our fathers, handed on, like some inheritance, by 
succession from the apostles and the saints who came after them.”244 
75. What does St. Basil the Great say about tradition? 
a. This saint refers to many quotations from the writings of the Fathers as witnesses of 
the orthodox faith. 
b. He also speaks of oral tradition as safeguarding the sound interpretation of the Holy 
Bible, which the heretics try to destroy. He says, “in truth, it is the faith that is the 
object of their war, and their intention, shared by all who oppose and hate sound 
teaching (1 Tim. 1:10) is to throw down the foundation of faith in Christ by dashing 
apostolic tradition to the ground and to obliterate it. On account of this, like true 
debtors they cry out for proofs from the Scriptures and dismiss the non -scriptural 
witness of the fathers as worthless.”245 
c. St. Basil  refers to tradition as our guide in sacraments and rites, saying: “Of the 
dogmas and proclamations that are guarded in the Church, we hold some from the 
teaching of the Scriptures, and others we have received in mystery [1 Cor. 2:7] as the 
teachings of the tradition of the apostles. Both hold the same power with respect to 
true religion. 
“No one would deny these points, at least no one who has even a little experience of 
ecclesiastical institutions. For if we attempt to reject non -scriptural customs as 
insignificant, we would, unaware, lose the very vital parts of the Gospel, and even 
more, we would establish the proclamation merely in name. 
“For instance — I will take the first and most common — who has learned through 
the Scriptures that those who hope in  the name of our Lord Jesus Christ are marked

65. How has the Holy Bible been preserved till today? 
The Holy Bible is the book of the Church, which we receive through the tradition of the 
Church. By tradition, our sacred books were canonized, confirming that they were divinely 
inspired. Origen the scholar says, “in all these questions we approve of nothing but what the 
Church approves of, namely only four canonical Gospels.” 203 St. Cyril of Jerusalem  says 
”Learn also diligently, and from the Church, what are the books of the Old Te stament, and 
what those of the New.” 204 So also St. Augustine: “For my part, I should not believe the 
gospel except as moved by the authority of the Catholic Church.”205 St. Basil the Great says, 
”For were we to attempt to reject such customs as have no writ ten authority, on the ground 
that the importance they possess is small, we should unintentionally injure the Gospel in its 
very vitals.”206 
It is important to note that while Church tradition testifies to the Holy Bible, and the Holy 
Bible is itself a part of the Church’s tradition, none of this diminishes the unique value of the 
Bible. Tradition defends the Bible’s nature as the word of God, the eternal divine revelation, 
which addresses not only the present age but also the ages to come.  
Although tradition testifies to the Holy Bible, it cannot be its judge. On the contrary, a 
tradition is only accepted if it is founded on the Bible; it cannot be accepted if it disagrees 
with the Holy Bible.207 
Moreover, the Holy Bible is for every believer, that he may experience it and personally 
taste its beauty, appreciating its value and inspiration. However, no one can by himself 
determine the divine inspiration of the Holy Bible and the presence of the Holy Spirit within 
the Bible — only the Holy Spirit who lives in t he Church can do that.  It is not through any 
individual effort of a human deciding alone, but through adherence to the judgment of the 
Church.208 
Finally, the close relationship between the Holy Bible and the tradition of the Church in 
no way extinguishes o ne’s personal feelings towards the Holy Bible. On the contrary, the 
tradition of the Church reinforces the personal approach, and requires of us that we live the 
Bible in no way isolated from the Church.

“gospel of salvation,” the “word of hearing” or the “God’s salvific work,” which he had 
received from the Church. He says, “Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the gospel which 
I preached unto you, which also you have received and wherein you stand … For I delivered 
unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to 
the scriptures; and that He was buried, and that He rose again on the third day according to 
the scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:1–4). “When you received the word of God which you heard of us, 
you received it not as the word of men but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectively 
works also in you who believe” (1 Thess. 2:13). Truly, the apostles received this gospel of 
the Church, not written on paper but through word of mouth, that they may deliver it to the 
Church by oral tradition, as well as written. 
On this note, Cyril Richardson says, “Hence Christian preaching was founded on the Old 
Testament and on the living tradition of Jesus, passed from mouth to mouth. This feeling for 
personal witness was very strong in the Early Church. Papias, for instance, records his disdain 
for books and his preference for ‘the living and abiding voice’.”196 
Many Western scholars are coming to appreciate this truth: oral tradition does not stand 
side by side with the written works as separate and distinct things; rather, they are one thing. 
What the Bible declares, the Church has received by oral tradition. 
F. F. Bruce, the professor of Biblical Criticism and Exegesis at the University of 
Manchester notes: “Whereas western Christians tend to set ‘script ure’ and ‘tradition’ over 
against each other, as though tradition were exclusively oral and not written, there is no 
reason why tradition should not take written form. If it is apostolic tradition, in due course it 
takes written form and becomes apostolic scripture. Whether Paul’s teaching was given orally 
or in writing, it equally carried apostolic authority; hence he can encourage the Thessalonian 
Christians to ‘stand firm and hold to the traditions which you were taught by us, either by 
word of mouth or by letter’ (2 Thess. 2:15).”197 
In The New Westminster Dictionary of the Bible we find, “The term (tradition), however, 
came to be used in a good sense of the apostolic teaching handed down in the Church either 
by the oral word or by letter.”198 
J. N. D. Kelly says, “by tradition the fathers usually mean doctrine which the Lord or His 
apostles committed to the Church, irrespective of whether it was handed down orally or in 
documents … The ancient meaning of the term is well illustrated by Athanasius’ reference199 
to ‘the actual original tradition, teaching and faith of the Catholic Church, which the Lord 
bestowed, the apostles proclaimed and the fathers safeguarded.’”200

l. There are hundreds of prophecies about the Lord Christ the Savior , from the 
beginning of creation until His incarnation , that are consistent with each other , and 
which even non-believing historians accept. These prophecies were not produced by 
the Christian Church  — they are part of the Old Testa ment and were preserved  by 
the Jews. They were only translated into other languages shortly before the coming 
of Christ, such as the  Greek Septuagint which was completed at the request of 
Ptolemy around the second century B. C. The Apostles used this trans lation in their 
preaching, especially the apostle Paul who preached to the gentiles.  
m. We can appreciate the wisdom of the Christian Church in that from the first century 
on, it has allowed every nation to worship in its own language and culture ; and yet, 
the Church enjoyed a wondrous unity until  the fifth century. No nation insisted that 
its language alone was holy  in Christian worship. With a spirit of love, many 
Christian writings were translated into th e languages of other nations, while 
preserving their nuance and their spiritual and theological purpose. Some Coptic 
and Arabic texts about the Copts were lost amidst the destruction and burning of 
churches and monasteries, but translations of some of thes e texts into Amharic, 
Greek, and other languages have survived.  
The believer does not deny the importance of the advancement of science, but he 
understands that these are theories that are liable to revision. For example: for a long time, 
scholars were c onfident that the Gospel of John was not written by St. John the Disciple, 
for its style was more like that of the second century. But when the Nag Hammadi 
papyruses were discovered in 1948, manuscripts from the first century were among them 
that exhibit t he same style as this gospel. Also, some scholars doubted the historical

Indeed, the Church received the “word of God” before it was written on paper. She 
enjoyed its good news and understood the deepest meaning of the word of God by the Holy 
Spirit through oral tradition, received not only by words but also as a way of life. She received 
this life more than twenty years before the New Testament began to be written . And when 
the evangelists and apostles did write the New Testament by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, 
the Church accepted it, venerated it, and understood it as the very life she had already been 
living. Thus, the Gospel is not a stranger to tradition , but its first component, for they both 
declare the “One Truth” and explain the nature of the Church. 
Perhaps one may ask whether oral tradition was annulled by the appearance of the books 
of the New Testament. We point to the apostles themselves who, in their letters to the early 
Christian communities, often reminded the believers of oral tradition from which they may 
gain an understanding of Christian truth. “Having many things to write to you, I did not wish 
to do so with paper and ink; but I hope to co me to you and speak face to face, that our joy 
may be full” (2 John 12). “I had many things to write, but I do not wish to write to you with 
pen and ink; but I hope to see you shortly, and we shall speak face to face” (3 John 13 –14). 
“And the rest I will s et in order when I come” (1 Cor. 11:34). “For this reason I left you in 
Crete, that you should set in order the things that are lacking and appoint elders in every city 
as I commanded you” (Titus 1:5). 
In many situations, the apostle Paul commands his disc iples to preserve the tradition, 
deliver it to others, and keep the traditions they were taught ― whether by word of mouth or 
by his epistles ― and to withdraw themselves “from every brother who walks disorderly and 
not according to the tradition which he received from us“ (2 Thess. 3:6). He also warns us to 
beware of every tradition of men which is inconsistent with the faith, “according to the basic 
principles of the world, and not according to Christ” (Col. 2:8). Moreover, in the early 
Church, converts to Christianity accepted the faith in many countries that had no versions of 
the Bible in their own languages and thus had no access to the truth except through oral 
tradition.201 
St. Irenaeus in the second century is the first to discuss the matter of tradition. He poses 
these questions: suppose we had no holy scripture, what would have happened? To whom 
should we turn? “Should we not have recourse to the most ancient Churches with which the 
apostles held constant intercourse, and learn from them what is certain and clear in regard to 
the present question? For how should it be if the apostles themselves had not left us writings? 
Would it not be necessary, [in that case,] to follow the course of the tradition which they 
handed down to those to whom they did commit the Churches?”202 
 
201 P. E. Hallett, A Catholic Dictionary. 15th ed. (London: Routledge & Kegan Paul, 1951): p. 782. 
202 St. Irenaeus of Lyon, Against Heresies 3.4.1 (ANF 1:417); J. F. Bethune-Baker, An Introduction to the 
Early History of Christian Doctrine (London: Methuen 1920): pp. 55–56.

Conclusion 
The Church and  Tradition are but two aspects of the life of Faith. They cannot be 
separated from each other, neither can we know one without the other. Through tradition, the 
Church comes into being, is acquainted with her Bridegroom, practices His saving work, and 
receives His divine mysteries. Through tradition, we come to know the Gospel of the Church, 
and we embrace it, preserve it, live by its rules, and preach it. Through tradition, we 
understand the sacramental life of the Church, with its liturgies, hymns, and ri tes. Through 
tradition, we meet the saints and fathers of the Church, learn of their lives in Christ Jesus and 
their writings, take the blessings of their prayers, and enjoy our fellowship with them in Christ 
Jesus. Through tradition we understand the cano ns of the Church and relate to its holy 
Councils and their works. 
In brief, tradition is the nervous system of the Church, and her life. Without it, she could 
not exist, nor practice the apostolic life, nor her continual renewal, nor her unity, nor live her 
authentic character.

records.question: Does the Coptic Orthodox Church accept the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary?
records.answer:
The Coptic Orthodox Church does not accept the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary, which is a belief held primarily by the Roman Catholic Church. The Immaculate Conception refers to the idea that Mary was conceived without original sin, meaning she was preserved from the stain of sin from the moment of her conception.

In the Coptic Orthodox understanding, while Mary is highly revered and honored as the Theotokos (meaning "God-bearer" or "Mother of God"), the Church does not teach that she was conceived without original sin. Instead, the Coptic tradition emphasizes her role as a faithful servant of God who accepted the divine will, as seen in the Annunciation where she responded positively to the angel Gabriel's message about bearing Christ (Luke 1:34-35) [3]. 

The Coptic Orthodox Church celebrates various feasts of the Virgin Mary, highlighting her significance in the life of Christ and the Church, but these celebrations do not include the doctrine of her Immaculate Conception. Instead, the focus is on her virtues, her role in the Incarnation, and her exemplary faith [1][2][6]. 

Thus, while Mary is honored as a pure and holy figure, the Coptic Orthodox Church maintains a different theological perspective regarding her conception compared to the Roman Catholic Church.

1079. What is the monthly Church cycle? 
Every month is sanctified  by our monthly commemoratio n of St. Mary the Mother of 
God, the Theotokos, on the 21 st of each Coptic month. We look up to St. Mary as a living 
role model for the faithful and the First Citizen of the Church of the Lord Christ, learning 
from her to live as those who carry the Lord C hrist wherever they go; He who establishes 
His kingdom in our depths.  
On the 29 th of every Coptic month, we commemorate the annunciation, nativity [or 
Christmas], and resurrection of Christ (except for the months of Tobe and Meshir) . With 
these commemorations, t he believer is dissolved into  love through his union with the 
Savior every hour, every day, every week, and every month. 
And we commemorate the chief of the army of the Lord, Archangel Michael, every 12th 
day of the Coptic month. Thus, the believer feels that he is a good soldier of our Lord Jesus 
(2 Tim. 2:3) and that he has joined the ranks of the heavenly powers. 
This is the happiness of the believer and his continual joy  on a daily, weekly, monthly, 
and annual basis. 
1080. What is the annual Church cycle? 
This cycle, in fact, subsumes all the days of the year. We celebrate the major and minor 
feasts of the Lord, the feasts of the Theotokos, the feasts of saints, the commemoration s of 
the consecration of churches, and the annual fasts. Through all of  this, we repeat in our 
depths the words  St. Athanasius  records in one of his Paschal letters: “‘Our Passover, 
Christ, is sacrificed’ (1 Cor. 5:7). Henceforth the feast of the Passover is ours.”618 
1081. What are the major feasts of our Lord? 
The feasts that celebrate important events in the life of our Lord can be categorized as 
major or minor, depending on their role in the salvation offered by the Lord Christ. The 
major feasts of the Lord  are below. Three have set dates in the Coptic calendar whi le the 
other four have moveable dates that change each year. 
a. Annunciation ( 29th Paremhotep / 7 th April). The evangelist repeat s the word 
“virgin” to affirm her virginity and declare that the Lord Christ was not born of the 
seed of man. This the prophet Ezekiel also declares (Ezek. 44:2–3). St. Mary heard 
the angel say to her , “The Lord is with you,” an expression with a unique meaning 
when applied to her. She tasted God’s presence on a unique level, for she carried the 
Word of God in her womb and offered Him her body and blood!  
 
618 St. Athanasius of Alexandria, Festal Letters 19.1 (NPNF II/4:544).

121. What does the phrase “was incarnate and became man” mean?  
The Son of God took for Himself a body from the womb of the Virgin, St. Mary and 
became a fetus without sin. He became a human being without ceasing being God. The 
evangelist says, “and the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). This God who became man 
intercedes for all humanity, offering Himself as a sacrifice for their sake. Therefore, the 
apostle Paul affirms that He became a man in truth, and not just as the illusion of a body, as 
the Gnostics claimed. He said, “For there is one God and one Mediator between God and 
men, the Man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).  
122. How is there only one nature in Christ?  
In Christ there is one nature of two natures, without mingling, without confusion, and 
without alteration. This is the nature of the Word who became Man. The Church equally 
rejects the Nestorian concept of Christ being two persons , and the faith of Eutyc hes who 
proclaimed that His humanity was swallowed up by His divinity or was dissolved in it.  
Through the unofficial and official dialogues between the Chalcedonian Orthodox and 
the non-Chalcedonian Orthodox, both affirmed their rejection of both the Nest orian and the 
Eutychian understandings. Further, both families asserted their rejection of any division or 
confusion between His divinity and His humanity.

the Virgin Mary”? 
The history of the people of God is marked by a number of miraculous births, such as: 
God’s promise to Abraham and Sarah of the birth of Isaac (Gen. 17:16–19); Hannah and the 
birth of Samuel the prophet (1 Sam. 1:1 –20); Manoah and his barren wife and the bi rth of 
their son Samson (Judg. 13:2–3); and Zacharias the priest and Elizabeth and the birth of John 
the Baptist (Luke 1:5–25). But a young, unknown virgin conceiving and bringing forth Jesus 
the Savior of the world surpassed all previous divine promises; for the Virgin bore in her 
body the promise of the salvation of the world. At the annunciation of the incarnation, the

Thomas, the Apostle, told them how he saw her pure body with the angels 
carrying it up to heaven. The Holy Spirit told them that God did not intend 
for her pure body to remain on earth, and the Lord Chr ist promised his pure 
disciples to let them see her in the flesh again, and they waited for this true 
promise until the 16 th of the month of Mesra when it was fulfilled. She lived 
on earth 60 years: she spent 12 years in the Temple, 30 years in the house o f 
the righteous Joseph the Carpenter, and 14 years in the house of St. John the 
Evangelist, according to the commandment of the Lord, who said to her: 
“Woman! Behold your son,” and to John: “Behold! Your mother” (John 
19:26-27). The first church, which was  built in the name of the Virgin St. 
Mary, was in the city of Philippi, in Greece. That happened after the 
preaching of St. Paul and St. Barnabas to the Gentiles in that city, and when 
many of them believed, they built that church. 
The Virgin St. Mary prov ided twice special blessings to the Land of 
Egypt. The first time when she fled to Egypt with the infant Jesus and St. 
Joseph the Carpenter, running away from king Herod who intended to kill the 
infant. the second time when she appeared in spiritual ways, inside and 
outside the domes of the church consecrated in her name in the area of El -
Zeitoun, in the suburbs of Cairo on the 2 nd of April 1968 (24 Baramhat 1684 
AM). Her appearances continued for many consecutive nights. 
The Church celebrates the Birthday of St. Mary on the 1 st of Bashons, her 
Entrance into the Temple on the 3 rd of Kiahk, her Departure on the 21 st of 
Toba, the Ascension of her body to Heaven on the 16th of Mesra, Building the 
first Church in her name on the 21 st of Paona, Consecrating the church in her 
name in the ‘Muĥarraq’ monastery, which the Lord Christ blessed by his 
presence along with His Apostles, on the 6 th of Hator and her Apparition in 
the church of El-Zeitoun on the 24th of Baramhat.

(b) The Coptic Catechism Through the Ages 
3. How did the Church preserve the correct faith through the ages? 
I greatly desired to present a Coptic Orthodox Catechism to reveal our Christian 
understanding concisely and briefly; particularly because, due to ecclesiastical and political 
circumstances, our Church was isolated from Western churches in the fifth century A. D. and 
remained so to a large extent up until the twentieth century, when she was accused by many 
in the West of adhering to Eutychianism. The Coptic Church, therefore, did not have the 
opportunity to reveal her true teachings through the writings of her Fathers and her liturgies. 
Despite the Church’s participation in many international theological conferences in recent 
years, insisting upon her rejection of Eutychianism, some sources continue to at tribute this 
heresy to our Church, of which the Church is completely innocent and strongly opposes 
through her liturgies and praises. 
In a certain dialogue with the Chalcedonian Orthodox Churches, theologians were 
surprised to observe that the liturgies an d praises that we enjoy to the present day lack even 
the slightest hint of Eutychianism, but rather, positively oppose it in a beautifully Christian 
manner; especially the daily Theotokias and those of the festal celebrations. Some of the 
theologians observed that they harmonize with the thought St. Cyril, or that perhaps he was 
their author.  
A Greek theologian once asked me whether we use the word “Theotokos” to describe St. 
Mary and was astonished to learn that it is a term beloved in Coptic texts in every age.  
4. What are the stages of development of Coptic Catechism through the ages? 
It is worth laying out the circumstances through which the Coptic Church has endured, 
from her foundation till the present day, that we may grasp the truth of her teachings, and 
benefit from her long experience over twenty centuries. 
Our Coptic Church has continuously faced persecution since the middle of the first 
century and until the present time. Thus, Mrs. Butcher, a Professor of History at Oxford 
University, expressed her amazement when she stated that the endurance of the Copts to this 
day is one of the wonders of the world. 
In the eighth century B. C., Isaiah the prophet anticipated the Coptic Church and wrote 
with the spirit of prophecy of her marvelous beginnings.  
The Church suffered many persecutions, even from fellow Christians. Such were the 
persecutions by the Emperors of Constantinople who persecuted her and appointed patriarchs

records.question: What is the filioque clause and why did the Coptic Church reject it?
records.answer:
The filioque clause refers to a phrase added to the Nicene Creed by the Western Church, stating that the Holy Spirit "proceeds from the Father and the Son." This addition has been a significant point of theological contention between the Eastern Orthodox and Western Catholic Churches. The Coptic Orthodox Church, which aligns more closely with the Eastern tradition, rejects this clause for several reasons.

Firstly, the Coptic Orthodox Church emphasizes the original wording of the Nicene Creed, which states that the Holy Spirit proceeds "from the Father." This reflects the belief in the distinct roles within the Holy Trinity: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Church holds that the addition of "and the Son" alters the understanding of the relationship within the Trinity, suggesting a dual source of the Holy Spirit that is not supported by the original texts or the teachings of the early Church Fathers, who emphasized the Father's role as the sole source of the Spirit's procession [3][4].

Additionally, the Coptic Orthodox Church views the filioque as a theological innovation that arose from a misunderstanding of the nature of the Trinity. The Church teaches that the Trinity consists of three distinct persons (hypostases) who are of one essence (ousia), and any alteration to the understanding of their relationships can lead to confusion and misinterpretation of the faith [2][6]. The Coptic tradition, rooted in the teachings of early Church Fathers like St. Athanasius and St. Cyril of Alexandria, maintains that the original formulation of the Creed is sufficient and reflects the true Orthodox faith [1][9].

In summary, the Coptic Orthodox Church rejects the filioque clause because it believes that it misrepresents the relationship within the Trinity, deviates from the original Nicene Creed, and introduces theological complexities that were not present in the early Church's understanding of the Holy Spirit's procession.

Catechism of the Coptic Orthodox Church – Volume 1  
102 
97. What is the Apostles’ Creed (Symbolum Apostolicum)? 
St. Hilary says, “We are compelled to attempt what is unattainable, to climb where we 
cannot reach, to speak w hat we cannot utter. Instead of the bare adoration of faith, we are 
compelled to trust the deep things of religion to the perils of human expression.”276 
The Lord Christ questioned his disciples about their faith in him, so Peter confessed that 
“He is the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). Perhaps this declaration of faith 
provided the main idea for the creation of a creed of faith for the Church that declares “the 
truth of the Lord Christ, the Savior.” Another time, the Lord gathered his disciples and gave 
them authority to preach, teach, and baptize, saying, “Go therefore and make disciples of all 
the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy 
Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), thus providing them with a formula  for a trinitarian creed related to 
baptism. Thus, the New Testament records for us a formula of faith in Christ and a formula 
of faith in the Trinity. These two formulas are the essence of the faith of the Church. 
F. L. Cross says of the Apostles’ Creed, “Though it is much later than the Apostolic age, 
it can so far claim to be Apostolic that its articles one and all express the faith of apostolic 
times.”277  
Patrology278 offers us many texts of creeds found in the writings of both Eastern and 
Western Fathers. Among these are creeds found in the writings of: Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, 
180 A.D.; Tertullian of Carthage, 200 A.D.; Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, 250 A.D.; Novatian 
of Rome, 250 A.D.; Origen of Alexandria, 250 A.D.; Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, 270 
A.D.; Lucian of Antioch, 300 A.D.; Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, 325 A.D.; Marcellus of 
Ancyra, 340 A.D.; Cyril of Jerusalem, 350 A.D.; Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, 3 74 A.D.; 
Rufinus of Aquileia, 390 A.D.; and the creed found in the Constitutions of the Holy Apostles. 
The Eastern texts differ from those of the West in that they are generally longer and more 
diverse. They have a metaphysical dimension (what lies beyond physical nature) and include 
a number of educational expressions in response to heresies that were widespread in the East. 
98. How did the Creed of the Church evolve?279 
In the apostolic era, as the Church set out to evangelize and preach salvation to the world, 
it was required of the catechumens to publicly confess their faith using a brief formula before 
being received as members of the body of Christ; that is, immediately before their baptism. 
 
276Anne Fremantle (ed.), A Treasury of Early Christianity (Viking Press, 1953): p. 325. 
277 F. L. Cross, The Early Christian Fathers (London: G. Duckworth, 1960): p. 89. The Apostles’ Creed is a 
different text to the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed used by the Coptic Orthodox Church.  
278 Patrology — the study of the Church Fathers’ lives and writings. Also known as patristics. 
279 Dom Gregory Dix, The Shape of the Liturgy (Bloomsbury, 2005): pp. 485–488; Philip Schaff, History of 
the Christian Church, Vol. II, Ch. 12; W. K. Lowther Clarke and Charles Harris, Liturgy and Worship 
(London: SPCK, 1932).

101. What did our Fathers of the Middle Ages transmit to us? 
The libraries of Europe overflow with medieval manuscripts from Egypt, in both the 
Coptic and Arabic languages, that reveal the theological richness of the Coptic Church of the 
Middle Ages. This motivates me to present a sample of their writings about the Creed.  
Abu Al-Majd ibn Yu’annis , a priest from Manyat Bani Khusib (now called Minya), 
who died in 1357 A.D., has an exposition of the Creed in about fifty large manuscript pages 
attributed to him. He wrote this at the request of Anba Gabriel, the bishop of Qus, in reply to 
a Jewish person who criticized the Creed saying, “Where did you get this text? And why 
have you inscribed it among the books of the church?” Thus, the book contains a collection 
of texts from the Old Testament to substantiate each of the Creed’s clauses.  
This work differs in its aims from other medieval Coptic expositions of the Creed: those 
of Severus ibn al-Muqaffa (around 940 A.D.); and a commentary at the beginning of the 
second chapter of Abu al-Barakat ibn Kabar’s  work titled Mișbâḥ al-ẓulma wa-îḍâḥ al-
khidma (The Lamp in the Shadows and the Illumination of Service , about 1310 A.D.). Abu 
al-Barakat quotes mostly from the New Testament. The Rev. Dr. Samir Khalil says that “the 
three Coptic commentaries complement each other in a felicitous manner.”282 
A summary of the text of Abu Al-Majd ibn Yu’annis’ exposition:283 
1. We believe in one God:  he cites the Torah (2 quotations), Isaiah  (2 quotations), 
Jeremiah, and the Gospel (2 quotations; these are the only quotations from the New 
Testament). 
2. The Father almighty, [Pantocrator] of all things visible and invisible:  quotations 
from Zechariah (2), Nahum, and the books of Kings. 
3. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only -begotten, born of the Father before all 
ages: quotations from Isaiah (2), David, Solomon (2), and Micah. 
4. Light of light, true God of true God, begotten not made:  quotations from Isaiah, 
Jeremiah, Isaiah, and David. 
5. For us, he came down from heaven: quotations from David, Isaiah (3), Esdras (Ezra), 
Jeremiah, David (2), an unnamed prophet, and Isaiah. 
6. He was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary:  quotations from Isaiah 
(2), Ezekiel (2), Nahum, Zephaniah, Zechariah, Daniel, and Isaiah (2). 
 
282 Samir Khalil, “Abu Al-Majd Ibn Yu’Annis” in The Coptic Encyclopedia, vol. 1, Atiya, Aziz Suryal, ed. 
(Macmillan, 1991), 21–23: p. 21. 
283 See Samir Khalil, “Abu Al-Majd Ibn Yu’Annis” in The Coptic Encyclopedia, vol. 1, Atiya, 
Aziz Suryal, ed. (Macmillan, 1991), 21–23: pp. 21–22.

a heretic.  
Some scholars have been in the habit of attributing violence to the Alexandrian fathers 
and theologians, even to Athanasius and Cyril. 
St. Dioscorus and the Council of Chalcedon: although the Council of Chalcedon was 
thought to have been convened to try Eutyches, in the event, its attention turned to attacking 
Pope Dioscorus of Alexandria, rather than the old monk. Eutyches was not even present at 
the council, having been exiled to north Syria before the council met.  
In fact, Dioscor us was condemned not because of any theological heresy, but due to 
political circumstances which dominated this council.  
The Greek Professor Fr. Romanides says, “Dioscorus was considered quite orthodox 
in his faith by such leading Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon as those represented 
by Anatolius of Constantinople.” 19 Metropolitan Methodios of Aksum also says, 
“Information, which we possess, does not depict Dioscorus as a heretic. From available 
information it is obvious that he was a good man and even Bishop Leo himself tried to take 
him to his side … Likewise Emperor Theodosius in a letter to Dioscorus calls him a man 
who radiates the Grace of God, a humble man and of orthodox faith. 
“Several times in the course of the Council Patriarch Diosco rus declared his faith. He 
was not condemned because he was heretical but because he refused to communicate with 
Leo, the Archbishop, and because he refused to come to the Council although he was invited 
to do so three times. 
“This evidence is sufficient for us to look for other reasons for Dioscorus’ condemnation. 
Rome was annoyed by the extraordinary vitality of the Church of Alexandria and its active 
Patriarch.”20  
The emperor accepted the council’s decision and exiled Pope Dioscorus to the island of 
Gangra in Asia Minor. He remained in exile for five years, occupying his time in guiding the 
lost and healing the sick. He departed to the glorious realm in the year 457 A. D. 
What impact did the Council of Chalcedon have on the catechism of the Church?  
a. The rise of strong theologians, such as Philoxenus of Mabbug, Pope Timothy, and the 
great teacher St. Severus of Antioch, who preserved the orthodoxy of the faith. Fr.

Review 10 (1965): p. 77.

Chalcedonian Churches” in Theological and Historical Studies: A Collection of Minor Works, ed. 
Methodios Fouyas (Athens, 1985): p. 15.
